paper.title: Vulnerable Code Search: Transferable Attack for Code Language Models
paper.summary: Reliable code retrieval is crucial for developer productivity and effective code reuse. However, current neural code language models (CLMs) powering search tools are susceptible to adversarial attacks targeting non-functional textual elements. In this paper, we introduce a programming language-agnostic, transferable, adversarial attack that exploits this CLM vulnerability. Our approach perturbs identifiers within a code snippet without altering the snippet's functionality to artificially align the code with a target query. We demonstrate that our attack, even when computed using smaller code embedding models, such as CodeT5+, is highly effective and transferable to larger, closed-source embedding models, like Voyage-code-3, or LLMs like Gemini-3.1-Pro. Our attack can increase the similarity between the query and arbitrary, irrelevant code snippets, consequently degrading key retrieval metrics such as the Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) of state-of-the-art models by up to 77%. The experimental results highlight the fragility of current code search methods and underscore the need for more robust, semantic-aware approaches.

analysis.problem_statement: Current neural code language models used for code retrieval are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that exploit non-functional textual elements to artificially inflate similarity scores between irrelevant code and queries.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Security and robustness of semantic search infrastructure in AI-assisted development tools.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper demonstrates that code search systems are fragile against transferable adversarial attacks that perturb identifiers without changing code functionality. By showing that attacks generated on small open-source models can degrade the performance of large, closed-source LLMs and embedding models, the work highlights a critical security gap in current developer productivity tools.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Degradation of Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR)
key_metrics.baseline: State-of-the-art code retrieval models (e.g., Voyage-code-3, Gemini-3.1-Pro)

technical_breakdown.method: A programming language-agnostic, transferable adversarial attack that perturbs code identifiers to align irrelevant snippets with target queries while preserving functionality.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Utilizes smaller code embedding models (e.g., CodeT5+) for attack generation, which is then transferred to larger, closed-source embedding models and LLMs.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Perturbation of non-functional textual elements (identifiers) to artificially increase semantic similarity between query and irrelevant code.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not specified in summary; relies on transferability from smaller models to avoid high computational costs of attacking large closed-source models directly.

paper.title: AsymSpec: Context-Asymmetric Speculative Decoding for Agentic LLMs
paper.summary: Agentic LLM pipelines face escalating inference costs as context accumulates across retrieval, tool use, and multi-turn interactions. To control latency, deployments routinely compress inputs, but this degrades task accuracy. Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates generation losslessly, yet it assumes the drafter and verifier share an identical context, preventing SD from resolving the accuracy-overhead trade-off. We propose AsymSpec, an asymmetric speculative decoding framework that breaks this symmetry: a lightweight drafter reads the full input while the large verifier operates on the compressed view. The drafter steers the verifier via a contrastive $δ$-fusion of logits, modulated by a divergence-aware acceptance gate that preserves verification stability and high draft acceptance rates. Evaluated across four agentic capabilities and two end-to-end agent benchmarks, AsymSpec reaches $\approx 90\%$ of full-context accuracy on average, delivering $1.3$--$1.7\times$ throughput speedups at $0.2$--$0.3\times$ the compute cost on isolated text capabilities. These results show that asymmetric context access yields substantial gains precisely when compression discards critical reasoning signals.

analysis.problem_statement: Standard speculative decoding cannot resolve the trade-off between inference latency and task accuracy in agentic LLMs because it requires the drafter and verifier to share identical context, preventing the use of compressed inputs for the large verifier.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Inference latency and compute cost associated with long-context processing in agentic pipelines.
analysis.executive_summary: AsymSpec addresses the high inference costs of agentic LLMs by decoupling the context requirements of the drafter and verifier in speculative decoding. By allowing a lightweight drafter to process full context while the large verifier uses a compressed view, it mitigates the accuracy loss typically caused by input compression. This approach enables significant throughput speedups without the substantial accuracy degradation seen in standard compression methods.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Throughput speedup and accuracy retention compared to full-context baseline
key_metrics.metric_value: 1.3-1.7x throughput speedup at 0.2-0.3x compute cost; ~90% of full-context accuracy
key_metrics.baseline: Full-context inference (no compression) and standard speculative decoding with identical context
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: Approximately 70-80% reduction in compute cost for isolated text capabilities while retaining ~90% accuracy

technical_breakdown.method: An asymmetric speculative decoding framework where the drafter and verifier operate on different context views, coordinated via logit fusion and a divergence-aware acceptance gate.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Lightweight drafter (full context), Large verifier (compressed context), Contrastive δ-fusion module, Divergence-aware acceptance gate.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: The drafter steers the verifier using a contrastive δ-fusion of logits. A divergence-aware acceptance gate modulates the process to preserve verification stability and maintain high draft acceptance rates despite context asymmetry.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Reduces compute cost to 0.2-0.3x of the baseline for isolated text capabilities, implying significant efficiency gains in the verification step by leveraging the smaller drafter for initial token generation on full context.

paper.title: ProgRouter: Online Progress-Guided Orchestration for Multi-Agent LLM Workflows under Quality-Cost Tradeoffs
paper.summary: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) workflows have emerged as a powerful paradigm for solving complex, open-ended tasks through collaborative reasoning among specialized LLM agents, but they incur substantial operating costs due to repeated LLM invocations and long-horizon context accumulation. Existing cascade routing methods make one-shot, query-level decisions and cannot adapt to the dynamic, state-dependent nature of multi-step workflows, in which the right LLM at each step depends on evolving task progress, remaining task difficulty, and cost-efficiency requirements. We present ProgRouter, an online progress-guided routing framework that adaptively selects LLM agents across workflow steps to preserve task-solving quality while adhering to time and cost budgets. ProgRouter introduces a multi-view task progress scorer that combines coarse workflow outcome regimes with fine-grained signals on subtask completion, progress trends, and workflow state quality. Then, a dual-path task progress predictor and an adaptive meta-gating mechanism estimate the progress gain for each candidate routed LLM. ProgRouter makes online step-wise routing decisions that balance progress gain, task time budgets, and long-term operating cost efficiency. Experiments on HumanEval Plus, MBPP, MATH-500, and ASQA, spanning agentic code generation, mathematical reasoning, and retrieval-augmented long-form question answering, demonstrate that ProgRouter reduces the operating cost relative to key baselines while maintaining strong task-solving performance.
paper.comment: Accepted in Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026. Index Terms: Collaborative agentic workflows, LLM agent orchestration, Quality-cost trade-off, Task progress prediction, Online decision-making

analysis.problem_statement: Existing cascade routing methods for multi-agent LLM workflows make static, one-shot decisions that fail to adapt to the dynamic, state-dependent nature of multi-step tasks, leading to suboptimal quality-cost tradeoffs.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: High operating costs and latency in multi-agent LLM workflows due to inefficient, non-adaptive agent selection and long-horizon context accumulation.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the significant financial and computational overhead of multi-agent LLM systems by introducing an online routing framework that dynamically selects agents based on real-time task progress. By balancing progress gain against time and cost budgets at each step, it enables scalable deployment of complex agentic workflows without sacrificing task-solving quality.

key_metrics.baseline: Key baselines including existing cascade routing methods

technical_breakdown.method: An online progress-guided routing framework that uses a multi-view task progress scorer to estimate progress gain for candidate LLMs, enabling step-wise adaptive decisions that balance quality, time, and cost.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Multi-view task progress scorer, dual-path task progress predictor, and adaptive meta-gating mechanism.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Combines coarse workflow outcome regimes with fine-grained signals on subtask completion, progress trends, and workflow state quality to estimate progress gain for each candidate routed LLM.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Online step-wise decision-making process; specific computational complexity or training time metrics are not provided in the metadata.

paper.title: XREPOTEST: Benchmarking Multilingual Repository-Level Unit Test Generation for Large Language Models
paper.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise for automated unit test generation, but existing evaluations largely rely on standalone settings and a narrow set of programming languages, overestimating real-world readiness. We introduce XREPOTEST, a multilingual repository-level benchmark for unit test generation spanning five underexplored languages: Rust, Go, Julia, PHP, and Ruby. XREPOTEST evaluates tests under realistic repository constraints using a containerized execution framework and multiple context augmentation strategies, including file-level, LSP-based, and retrieval-based context. Beyond standard metrics such as test pass rate and coverage, we propose Invocation Rate (IR) to assess whether generated tests meaningfully exercise the intended functionality. Experiments with 14 state-of-the-art LLMs, including Claude 4.5, GPT-5.2, DeepSeek V4-Pro, and Qwen families, reveal a substantial gap between standalone and repository-level performance, as well as trade-offs between richer context and test reliability. Overall, XREPOTEST provides a challenging and informative benchmark to advance scalable and robust unit test generation in realistic software environments. The dataset and code are publicly available at: https://github.com/solis-team/XRepoTest

analysis.problem_statement: Existing evaluations of LLM-based unit test generation rely on standalone, single-file settings and a narrow set of languages, leading to an overestimation of model readiness for realistic, multilingual repository-level software environments.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Evaluation realism and generalization gap in code generation benchmarks, specifically regarding repository-level context integration and multilingual support.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical disconnect between academic code generation benchmarks and real-world software engineering by introducing a multilingual, repository-level benchmark. It highlights that current state-of-the-art LLMs perform significantly worse in realistic repository contexts compared to standalone settings, necessitating new evaluation standards for robust automated testing.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Gap between standalone and repository-level performance and trade-offs in context augmentation strategies
key_metrics.baseline: Standalone unit test generation settings and narrow language benchmarks

technical_breakdown.method: A containerized execution framework evaluates generated tests under realistic repository constraints across five underexplored languages (Rust, Go, Julia, PHP, Ruby), utilizing multiple context augmentation strategies.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Benchmark infrastructure comprising a containerized execution environment, a multilingual dataset, and a context retrieval system supporting file-level, LSP-based, and retrieval-based strategies.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Introduces a new metric called Invocation Rate (IR) to assess functional exercise of intended code, alongside standard test pass rate and coverage metrics. Experiments involve 14 state-of-the-art LLMs including Claude 4.5, GPT-5.2, DeepSeek V4-Pro, and Qwen families.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not specified in abstract

paper.title: One Form to Transfer Them All: Pretraining Multilingual Language Models Beyond Native Orthography
paper.summary: Multilingual language models transfer knowledge across languages through shared subword vocabulary, a mechanism that breaks down when related languages use different writing systems. Prior work addresses this via script equalization (romanization or IPA transcription), but direct comparisons are rare; the focus has been on encoder-only models, with most work adapting existing pretrained models. We systematically compare different input representations in autoregressive multilingual pretraining, comparing orthographic text, IPA, and romanization in a controlled setup across three scales (467M, 709M, and 1.03B) on eight languages in four typologically motivated pairs. Across a wide range of downstream tasks on seen and unseen languages, romanized pretraining yields the strongest cross-lingual transfer, and the advantage over text widens with scale. IPA improves over text in most settings but trails romanization. Surprisingly, finetuning a text-pretrained model on romanized data hurts performance on languages already covered by the base model, only marginally helping when the model lacks script coverage. Our results indicate that for multilingual models spanning typologically diverse scripts, to obtain maximum benefits, romanization should be treated as a core design choice applied at pretraining rather than a post hoc fix.

analysis.problem_statement: Multilingual language models fail to effectively transfer knowledge across related languages that use different writing systems due to disjoint subword vocabularies.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Cross-lingual transfer efficiency in multilingual autoregressive pretraining when scripts are typologically diverse.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper demonstrates that treating romanization as a core pretraining design choice, rather than a post-hoc adaptation, significantly enhances cross-lingual transfer in autoregressive models. It provides a systematic comparison of orthographic, IPA, and romanized inputs, showing that romanized pretraining yields the strongest transfer benefits, particularly as model scale increases.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Cross-lingual transfer performance on downstream tasks for seen and unseen languages
key_metrics.baseline: Orthographic text pretraining and IPA transcription
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: Not quantified in abstract; advantage over text widens with scale

technical_breakdown.method: Controlled comparison of input representations (orthographic, IPA, romanization) in autoregressive multilingual pretraining across three model scales (467M, 709M, 1.03B) and eight languages in four typologically motivated pairs.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Autoregressive multilingual language models (decoder-only), tested at 467M, 709M, and 1.03B parameter scales.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Pretraining on romanized, IPA, or orthographic text; evaluation on downstream tasks for seen and unseen languages; analysis of finetuning text-pretrained models on romanized data.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Training costs scale with model size (467M to 1.03B parameters); no specific FLOPs or time metrics provided in the abstract.

paper.title: From Passive Response to Proactive Correction: Enhancing LLM Robustness Against Input Fact Perturbations
paper.summary: Large language models (LLMs) frequently produce confident yet factually incorrect responses when user inputs contain misleading premises, a phenomenon we attribute to fact perturbations in the input. Existing approaches to hallucination mitigation typically assume reliable user inputs, overlooking how such factual errors can actively mislead model reasoning. To address this vulnerability, we propose DEDUCE, a three-stage framework that transforms LLMs from passive responders into proactive error correctors. DEDUCE operates in three stages: (1) detect errors through fine-grained fact extraction and verification; (2) devise correction strategies via multi perspective deliberation; and (3) correct misconceptions while delivering reliable answers. We also present MisFactQA, a dataset containing factual errors of varying degrees, and propose new metrics for evaluating model robustness. Experiments on TruthfulQA, FalseQA, and our MisFactQA benchmark demonstrate that DEDUCE significantly improves both accuracy and error correction capability. Consistent gains across Qwen, LLaMA, and Gemma families confirm its effectiveness and scalability.
paper.comment: Accepted to the Main Conference of EMNLP 2026

analysis.problem_statement: LLMs often generate confident but factually incorrect responses when user inputs contain misleading premises or factual errors, a vulnerability not adequately addressed by existing hallucination mitigation methods that assume reliable inputs.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Input robustness and factuality under adversarial or erroneous user premises (hallucination mitigation via proactive correction).
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses a critical gap in LLM reliability where models fail to detect and correct factual errors embedded in user queries, leading to compounded reasoning failures. By introducing DEDUCE, a framework that shifts LLMs from passive responders to proactive correctors, it enhances robustness against input fact perturbations. The inclusion of the MisFactQA dataset and new robustness metrics provides a standardized way to evaluate this specific failure mode across diverse model families.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Improvement in accuracy and error correction capability on TruthfulQA, FalseQA, and MisFactQA benchmarks
key_metrics.baseline: Standard LLM responses without proactive correction (Qwen, LLaMA, Gemma families)

technical_breakdown.method: A three-stage framework (DEDUCE) that detects input errors, devises correction strategies, and corrects misconceptions to deliver reliable answers.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Three-stage pipeline: (1) Fine-grained fact extraction and verification for error detection; (2) Multi-perspective deliberation for strategy formulation; (3) Misconception correction and answer generation.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses fine-grained fact extraction, verification mechanisms, and multi-perspective deliberation to handle varying degrees of factual errors in inputs.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not specified, but implies additional inference steps for detection and deliberation, likely increasing latency compared to single-pass generation.

paper.title: Unlocking Multimodal Protein Language Models at Inference Time
paper.summary: Multimodal protein language models (pLMs) learn joint protein sequence-structure distributions, and their generation performance should also depend critically on inference-time sampling strategies. Yet prior work has focused more on model training than on how inference-time strategies behave. In this paper, we establish a three-stage investigation framework to empirically study the inference design space of multimodal pLMs across three representative pLMs and four fundamental tasks. We evaluate vanilla sampling, task-specific classifier-free guidance, and reward-guided beam search on multimodal pLMs, corresponding to controls over sampling distributions, per-step logits, and parallel trajectories. Throughout the complementary advancements centered on exploration-exploitation trade-off, we (1) reveal the suboptimality of default inference protocols and identify task-oriented sampling preferences; (2) observe substantial quantitative gains across tasks, consistently boosting the upper bound performance of multimodal pLMs without updating model parameters; (3) derive conclusions about base models that differ from prior consensus.

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the lack of empirical understanding regarding how inference-time sampling strategies impact the generation performance of multimodal protein language models.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Inference efficiency and optimization; specifically, the suboptimality of default inference protocols in generative AI models.
analysis.executive_summary: This work shifts focus from training to inference, demonstrating that standard sampling methods for multimodal protein language models are suboptimal. By introducing a framework to evaluate task-specific classifier-free guidance and reward-guided beam search, the paper shows that inference-time adjustments can significantly boost performance without parameter updates.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Quantitative gains in generation performance across four fundamental tasks
key_metrics.baseline: Vanilla sampling and default inference protocols

technical_breakdown.method: A three-stage investigation framework evaluating inference design space across three representative pLMs and four tasks, comparing vanilla sampling, task-specific classifier-free guidance, and reward-guided beam search.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Multimodal protein language models (pLMs) that learn joint protein sequence-structure distributions.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Controls over sampling distributions, per-step logits, and parallel trajectories; exploration-exploitation trade-off analysis.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: No model parameter updates required; computational overhead associated with beam search and guidance mechanisms at inference time.

paper.title: Localize-Then-Decide Guarantees for LLM Judgments
paper.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as evaluators to assess output quality and preference alignment, yet providing reliable guarantees of agreement with human judgments remains challenging. Recent work introduces confidence-thresholding methods that provide such guarantees for pairwise comparisons, relying on the assumption that higher estimated confidence implies lower disagreement risk with humans. However, this assumption can break down when the number of candidate responses increases, since distributing probability mass across many alternatives can distort confidence estimates. To address this issue, we propose a Localize-Then-Decide framework. First, conformal prediction localizes a small shortlist that contains the human-preferred response with high probability. Then, a calibrated confidence-based rule selectively chooses a single response from this shortlist or abstains. This design restores the monotonic relationship between confidence and disagreement risk and enables high-probability agreement guarantees. Experiments with multiple candidate sizes across several datasets and judge LLMs demonstrate that our framework consistently achieves higher guarantee success rates and substantially higher coverage than single-stage baselines.
paper.comment: Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026. Code: https://github.com/llm2409/Localize-Then-Decide

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the failure of confidence-thresholding methods to provide reliable agreement guarantees with human judgments when the number of candidate responses increases, due to the distortion of confidence estimates by probability mass distribution.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Reliability and calibration of LLM-based evaluators in multi-candidate selection tasks.
analysis.executive_summary: As LLMs are increasingly deployed as automated judges, ensuring their decisions align with human preferences is critical for trust and deployment. This paper identifies a critical flaw in existing confidence-based guarantees for multi-candidate scenarios and proposes a two-stage framework that restores the monotonic relationship between confidence and risk. This enables high-probability agreement guarantees with significantly higher coverage than previous single-stage methods.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Guarantee success rate and coverage
key_metrics.baseline: Single-stage confidence-thresholding baselines

technical_breakdown.method: A Localize-Then-Decide framework that first uses conformal prediction to generate a shortlist containing the human-preferred response with high probability, then applies a calibrated confidence-based rule to select a single response or abstain.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Two-stage pipeline: 1) Localization stage using conformal prediction to narrow down candidates; 2) Decision stage using a calibrated confidence rule on the shortlist.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Conformal prediction for shortlist generation; calibrated confidence-based decision rule; handling of probability mass distribution across multiple alternatives.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not specified in abstract, but implies additional computational overhead for conformal prediction and calibration compared to single-stage methods.

paper.title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Aggregation in Semi-Supervised Federated Learning with non-IID Data
paper.summary: Federated Learning (FL) enables distributed training of machine learning models while preserving data privacy. However, FL struggles with heterogeneous, non-IID client data distributions, resulting in sub-optimal and biased global models. In this paper, we propose pFedMARL, a novel approach leveraging Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) with Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) to dynamically adapt aggregation strategies in FL settings. Our method employs a server-side agent adjusting client contributions to optimize global model robustness and client-side agents balancing global and local updates to personalize models effectively without pre-training. We demonstrate superior performance of pFedMARL for training a semi-supervised audio spectrogram transformer, matching or outperforming FedAvg, Ditto, and local training approaches across multiple non-IID scenarios and in the presence of adversarial clients. Our results indicate that pFedMARL actively improves accuracy, robustness, and fairness, making it suitable for real-world deployments.
paper.comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, ICASSP 2026 - 2026 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP)

analysis.problem_statement: Federated Learning suffers from sub-optimal and biased global models when client data distributions are heterogeneous and non-IID, particularly in the presence of adversarial clients.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Data heterogeneity and non-IID distribution in distributed/edge learning environments.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical challenge of model degradation in Federated Learning caused by non-IID data by introducing a reinforcement learning-based adaptive aggregation strategy. By dynamically adjusting client contributions and balancing local versus global updates, the method enhances robustness and fairness without requiring pre-training, making it suitable for real-world, privacy-preserving deployments.

key_metrics.baseline: FedAvg, Ditto, and local training

paper.title: Learning New Facts with QLoRA: An Acquisition-Retention Frontier
paper.summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning is often assumed to preserve pretrained capabilities because it updates only a small number of parameters. We show that this assumption depends strongly on adapter capacity. We study factual acquisition in a controlled OpenStreetMap-derived benchmark where Qwen3-4B must acquire anonymized geographic associations while retaining unrelated capabilities. Comparing full fine-tuning (FFT) with quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) at ranks 8, 16, 32, and 64, we find that rank induces a clear acquisition--retention frontier. Low-rank QLoRA preserves out-of-domain (OOD) performance but acquires fewer facts, whereas higher ranks improve same-fact paraphrase generalization at an increasing cost in performance on unrelated benchmarks. FFT behaves as a conservative baseline: it retains general capabilities well, but does not reach the highest factual-acquisition regime. Distributional, weight-space, and spectral diagnostics mirror this behavioral trade-off, with higher-rank QLoRA moving farther from the pretrained model. A separate math adaptation experiment shows a weaker frontier, suggesting that the effect is most pronounced when adaptation must install new factual associations rather than reinforce skills already supported by pretraining. Code and data are available at https://github.com/zhngstl/new_facts_forgetting.

analysis.problem_statement: The paper investigates the trade-off between acquiring new factual knowledge and retaining pre-existing capabilities in parameter-efficient fine-tuning, specifically demonstrating that this trade-off is governed by the rank of the LoRA adapter.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Catastrophic forgetting and the capacity limits of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) in balancing new knowledge acquisition with general capability retention.
analysis.executive_summary: This work challenges the assumption that low-rank adaptation inherently preserves pretrained capabilities, revealing that adapter rank dictates a clear acquisition-retention frontier. It demonstrates that while low-rank QLoRA preserves out-of-domain performance, it limits factual acquisition, whereas higher ranks improve generalization to new facts at the cost of degrading unrelated capabilities.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Acquisition-Retention Frontier performance (trade-off between new fact acquisition and OOD retention)
key_metrics.metric_value: Qualitative frontier observed across ranks 8, 16, 32, and 64
key_metrics.baseline: Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) and lower-rank QLoRA configurations
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: Not quantified as a single percentage; characterized as a trade-off curve

technical_breakdown.method: Comparative analysis of Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) and Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) at varying ranks (8, 16, 32, 64) on a controlled factual acquisition benchmark.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Qwen3-4B base model with QLoRA adapters of variable rank; OpenStreetMap-derived benchmark for geographic associations.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Use of distributional, weight-space, and spectral diagnostics to correlate behavioral trade-offs with model deviation from the pretrained state; controlled anonymization of geographic data to test factual association.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Computational cost scales with adapter rank; higher ranks require more memory and compute for the adapter parameters but remain efficient compared to full fine-tuning.

paper.title: Overview of SHROOM-Visions 2026: A Shared Task on Hallucination Detection in Large Vision-Language Models
paper.summary: In 2026, we held the fourth iteration of the SHROOM Shared Task series: SHROOM-Visions (\textbf{S}hared-task on \textbf{H}allucinations and \textbf{R}elated \textbf{O}bservable \textbf{O}vergeneration \textbf{M}istakes in \textbf{Vision} language model\textbf{s}), which is hosted at the UncertaiNLP Workshop co-located with EMNLP 2026. Following the success of the 2024 and 2025 tasks, this time we aim to tackle hallucinations through a model-agnostic detection task focused on large vision-language models. Building on the recently introduced SHEEP dataset, designed for long-term evaluation across model generations, the task invites participants to detect and classify fine-grained hallucination spans in image-conditioned text generation (VQA, image captioning, etc.). The evaluation uses a five-class taxonomy of hallucinations spanning four languages: Chinese, English, French, and Italian. The shared task generated strong interest in the NLP community worldwide, with 27 teams contributing 600+ system submissions. The best systems achieve average scores of 0.58 in character-level correlation, 0.46 in label-conditioned correlation, and 0.51 in intersection-over-union (IoU) across four languages, outperforming the baselines by 30-40 points.

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the challenge of detecting and classifying fine-grained hallucination spans in image-conditioned text generation by large vision-language models (VLMs) across multiple languages.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Reliability and factual grounding in multimodal AI systems, specifically the tendency of VLMs to generate content not supported by visual input (hallucinations).
analysis.executive_summary: This shared task provides a standardized, model-agnostic benchmark for evaluating hallucination detection in VLMs, which is critical for deploying these models in safety-critical applications. By introducing a multilingual, fine-grained taxonomy and a long-term evaluation dataset (SHEEP), it enables the community to track progress in reducing observable overgeneration mistakes across different model generations.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Average scores in character-level correlation, label-conditioned correlation, and Intersection-over-Union (IoU) across four languages.
key_metrics.baseline: Baseline systems provided for the shared task.

technical_breakdown.method: A model-agnostic detection task where participants submit systems to identify and classify hallucination spans within generated text conditioned on images.
technical_breakdown.architecture: The task framework relies on the SHEEP dataset and a five-class hallucination taxonomy; participant architectures are varied but generally involve span detection and classification modules applied to VLM outputs.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Evaluation is conducted across four languages (Chinese, English, French, Italian) using metrics for span overlap (IoU) and label accuracy. The dataset is designed for long-term evaluation to accommodate evolving model generations.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not specified in the abstract; complexity varies by participant system, but the evaluation infrastructure supports 600+ submissions from 27 teams.

paper.title: Think-Probe-Respond: Improving Large Language Models as Judges of Research Idea Novelty
paper.summary: Automated novelty judgment can accelerate scientific discovery by enabling efficient evaluation, refinement, and comparison of research ideas. While large language models are increasingly adopted for this task, we investigate a previously overlooked limitation in their judgment capabilities: despite generating reasoning rationales that closely mirror those of human experts, their final novelty judgments often diverge substantially. We demonstrate that this miscalibration stems from a systematic bias towards judging ideas as "medium novel". To mitigate this, we propose Think-Probe-Respond (TPR), a lightweight approach that probes latent novelty judgments from hidden states during the reasoning phase and uses the probed judgments to condition the final response. Across strong baselines, TPR improves novelty judgment performance by 22.30% and successfully mitigates the prevalent "medium novelty" bias.

analysis.problem_statement: Large language models exhibit a systematic miscalibration bias towards assigning 'medium' novelty scores to research ideas, despite generating reasoning rationales that align with human experts.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Reliability and calibration of LLM-based automated evaluation for scientific discovery.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses a critical gap in using LLMs as judges for research novelty, where final judgments diverge from the model's own expert-like reasoning. By identifying and mitigating a specific 'medium novelty' bias, the proposed method enhances the trustworthiness of automated scientific evaluation pipelines.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Improvement in novelty judgment performance
key_metrics.baseline: Strong baselines

technical_breakdown.method: Think-Probe-Respond (TPR) probes latent novelty judgments from hidden states during the reasoning phase and uses these probed judgments to condition the final response generation.
technical_breakdown.architecture: A lightweight post-hoc or intermediate intervention layer that accesses hidden states during the reasoning chain to influence the final output.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Extraction of latent judgments from hidden states; conditioning the final response generation on these probed values to counteract the medium-novelty bias.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Described as a 'lightweight approach', implying low additional computational overhead compared to full retraining or complex multi-agent systems.

paper.title: Reconstructing the Right Episode: Evaluating Interleaved Conversational Memory Beyond Long Context
paper.summary: Conversations with chat assistants increasingly span many topics in a single long-running thread, challenging memory systems. Existing long-context and memory benchmarks often expose session or topic boundaries, or probe direct personal-memory questions. These settings understate a harder assistant-memory regime: a flat mixed-topic thread where the system must infer which earlier episode makes a later task decision valid. We introduce SCALE-QA, a constraint-grounded task QA benchmark for flat unsegmented threads targeting episode integrity failure. The dataset contains 3,000 audited questions across 10 domains, uses deterministic four-way multiple-choice grading, and includes a deterministic runtime builder; experiments use all 3,000 questions through 128k and a stratified 400-question diagnostic at 1M. SCALE-QA questions are ordinary task-oriented requests whose correct answer depends on causally related evidence introduced earlier in the conversation. We also propose Temporal-Semantic Interleaved Memory Reconstruction (TSIM), which segments the turn stream into coherent episodes and indexes them through a hierarchical multi-view memory stack with deterministic episode-level summary and cluster-routing views. Experiments show that SCALE-QA challenges strong RAG baselines and long-context LLMs alike; across three open-source and proprietary LLM backends, TSIM achieves the highest accuracy in every backend setting, gaining 5.6-17.6 accuracy points over the strongest corresponding baseline.
paper.comment: 19 pages, 6 figures, 30 tables. Accepted to the Main Conference of EMNLP 2026

analysis.problem_statement: Existing long-context and memory benchmarks fail to adequately test the ability of AI assistants to identify and utilize specific, causally relevant episodes within flat, unsegmented, mixed-topic conversation threads.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Ineffective retrieval and reasoning over unstructured, interleaved conversational history in long-context scenarios.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses a critical gap in evaluating LLM memory by introducing SCALE-QA, a benchmark that tests 'episode integrity' in flat, mixed-topic threads where topic boundaries are not explicit. It proposes TSIM, a hierarchical memory architecture that segments turns into coherent episodes, significantly outperforming standard RAG and long-context baselines. This is crucial for developing reliable personal assistants that must navigate complex, multi-topic user histories without explicit structural cues.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Accuracy improvement over strongest baseline
key_metrics.baseline: Strongest corresponding RAG and long-context LLM baselines
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: Not explicitly quantified as a percentage, but absolute accuracy points gained

technical_breakdown.method: TSIM segments the turn stream into coherent episodes and indexes them using a hierarchical multi-view memory stack.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Hierarchical multi-view memory stack with deterministic episode-level summary and cluster-routing views.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Deterministic runtime builder for the benchmark; four-way multiple-choice grading; stratified sampling for 1M token diagnostics.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not specified in the abstract, but implies overhead for episode segmentation and hierarchical indexing compared to flat context processing.

paper.title: RetrievalRouter: Joint Modality and Architecture Selection for Document Retrieval
paper.summary: Document retrieval increasingly supports high-stakes information access in finance, healthcare, and law. Modern retrieval pipelines vary both in modality (text or multimodal) and in retrieval architecture (dense or late-interaction). These choices impose a hard compromise: the most effective pipelines are too slow and expensive to run at scale, while the fastest fail to retrieve evidence from complex documents. Practitioners must therefore choose between missed evidence and unusable latency, with no principled basis for adapting that choice at the query level. We show that this compromise is unnecessary. Not every query requires the same pipeline. Across benchmarks spanning financial and scientific corpora, no static pipeline dominates. We introduce RetrievalRouter, a lightweight query-aware router that learns, from the query text alone, which retrieval pipeline best fits each query. A single tunable parameter exposes the full accuracy-latency frontier, and for every static baseline, RetrievalRouter offers an operating point that is simultaneously more accurate and faster. Against the best static baseline, RetrievalRouter is 2.5% more accurate and 12.4 times faster. Furthermore, compared with prior adaptive strategy selection methods, RetrievalRouter achieves significantly higher nDCG@5 across accuracy-oriented settings, while matching or numerically outperforming them on both nDCG@5 and latency in latency-oriented settings. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/emrekuruu/retrieval-router.

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the lack of a principled, query-level mechanism to dynamically select between different document retrieval pipelines (varying by modality and architecture) to optimize the trade-off between retrieval accuracy and latency.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Inefficiency in static retrieval pipelines that force a hard compromise between high-accuracy (slow/expensive) and high-speed (low-accuracy) methods, preventing optimal resource allocation per query.
analysis.executive_summary: This work demonstrates that a single static retrieval pipeline is suboptimal across diverse queries in high-stakes domains like finance and healthcare. By introducing a lightweight router that selects the best pipeline based solely on query text, it enables systems to operate on the full accuracy-latency frontier, offering simultaneous improvements in both speed and precision compared to fixed baselines.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Simultaneous improvement in accuracy (nDCG) and latency reduction compared to the best static baseline.
key_metrics.baseline: Best static retrieval pipeline baseline

technical_breakdown.method: A lightweight, query-aware routing mechanism that predicts the optimal retrieval pipeline (modality and architecture combination) for each individual query based on the input text.
technical_breakdown.architecture: RetrievalRouter component that interfaces with a set of heterogeneous retrieval pipelines (dense vs. late-interaction, text vs. multimodal).
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: The router is trained to learn the mapping from query features to pipeline selection, exposing a single tunable parameter that controls the operating point on the accuracy-latency frontier. It outperforms prior adaptive strategy selection methods in nDCG@5.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Described as 'lightweight,' implying low computational overhead for the routing decision itself, allowing for real-time adaptation without significant additional latency compared to static execution.

paper.title: Plans You Can Check: Verifier-Grounded Learning of an Open-Weight Planner for Executable Video-Editing
paper.summary: Practical video editing is not only pixel generation: an editor must turn a brief, a clip pool, music metadata, and hard constraints into an executable timeline. We study this decision layer as \emph{executable video-editing planning} and introduce RefineCut, which, unlike workflow systems that wrap a prompted frontier model, trains a compact open-weight planner for it. The planner edits a typed timeline through structured patches covering clip selection, trimming, ordering, transitions, and duration and music alignment; a deterministic verifier applies each patch and checks it against an explicit constraint ledger. Because editing has no single ground-truth repair, we do not imitate teachers directly: RefineCut replays every multi-teacher branch through the verifier and keeps verifier-best repairs as supervision. A second stage, RefineCut-Evo, lets the student score its own repairs with the verifier and a task rubric and trains on high-margin preference pairs, so the final $8$B planner runs in a closed verifier loop with no teacher calls at inference. On RefineCut-Bench ($3{,}578$ tasks, $7{,}971$ captioned clips, $499$ music tracks, explicit ledgers), verifier-replayed distillation lifts the planner from $0.620$ to $0.858$ on the protocol-specific Video-Editing Score and RefineCut-Evo reaches $0.924$; the gain transfers to Llama-3.1-8B and GLM-4-9B, and in the same closed loop the $8$B planner matches or exceeds its frontier teachers. Code and RefineCut-Bench are publicly released; see the Data Availability statement.
paper.comment: Accepted to the Main Conference of EMNLP '26

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the challenge of training a compact, open-weight planner that can generate executable video-editing timelines by satisfying hard constraints and aligning with creative briefs, without relying on frontier model inference at deployment.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Reduces dependency on proprietary, high-cost frontier LLMs for complex, constraint-satisfying planning tasks by distilling their capabilities into a smaller, self-contained open-weight model.
analysis.executive_summary: This work shifts video editing from simple pixel generation to structured, constraint-driven planning, enabling efficient local deployment of high-quality editors. By using a deterministic verifier to filter and refine multi-teacher outputs, it creates a robust training signal that allows an 8B model to match or exceed the performance of larger frontier models in a closed loop.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Video-Editing Score on RefineCut-Bench
key_metrics.baseline: Initial planner performance of 0.620

technical_breakdown.method: Verifier-Grounded Learning: The system replays multi-teacher branches through a deterministic verifier, keeping only verifier-best repairs as supervision. A second stage (RefineCut-Evo) uses self-scoring via the verifier and a task rubric to train on high-margin preference pairs.
technical_breakdown.architecture: An 8B open-weight planner that edits a typed timeline using structured patches (clip selection, trimming, ordering, transitions, alignment). It operates in a closed loop with a deterministic verifier that checks patches against an explicit constraint ledger.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses structured patches for timeline editing rather than free-text generation. Employs a two-stage training process: 1) Verifier-replayed distillation from multiple teachers, 2) Self-improvement via high-margin preference pairs scored by the verifier and task rubric. No teacher calls are made during inference.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: The 8B planner is designed for efficient inference without frontier model calls. Training involves replaying and filtering multi-teacher branches, which adds computational overhead during the distillation phase but reduces inference costs significantly.

paper.title: AWM: Answerable Working Memory for Long-Document VQA Agents
paper.summary: Long-document visual question answering increasingly relies on VLM agents that retrieve candidate pages, inspect page images, write findings to working memory, and synthesize answers. Working memory should carry answer-supporting evidence across page inspections for later grounded answering, yet existing evaluation mainly checks final-answer correctness and evidence-page access. This creates a memory-quality blind spot: an agent may reach the right page and answer correctly while leaving behind memory too generic or incomplete to support answering once page context is removed. We introduce \emph{memory-only answerability}, a diagnostic that asks whether a reader can answer from the question and terminal working memory alone. Building on this diagnostic, \emph{Answerable Working Memory} (AWM) treats terminal working memory as an answerable evidence artifact, and AWM-GRPO incorporates this signal into the GRPO reward while preserving final-answer priority. Under GRPO, this reward assigns higher advantages to answer-correct trajectories whose terminal working memory remains answerable. On \textsc{MMLongBench-Doc}, even when gold evidence pages are provided, 42.5\% of correct answers still cannot be answered from terminal working memory alone. AWM-GRPO improves final-answer accuracy over the RAG baseline by 8.1 and 11.9 points on \textsc{MMLongBench-Doc} and \textsc{LongDocURL} and reduces the memory-missing-correct rate by 2.7 points over answer-only GRPO.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing long-document VQA agents often produce final answers that are correct but rely on transient page context, leaving their terminal working memory too generic or incomplete to support answering if the visual context is removed.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Memory quality and evidence retention in multi-step agentic reasoning pipelines.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses a critical 'memory-quality blind spot' in VLM agents where standard evaluations ignore whether the agent's internal state is sufficient for grounded reasoning. By introducing a diagnostic for 'memory-only answerability' and integrating it into the GRPO reward function, the method ensures that agents not only find the right information but also consolidate it into a robust, self-contained evidence artifact.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Final-answer accuracy improvement over RAG baseline
key_metrics.metric_value: 8.1 points on MMLongBench-Doc and 11.9 points on LongDocURL
key_metrics.baseline: RAG baseline
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: Not explicitly quantified as a percentage in the summary, but absolute point gains are 8.1 and 11.9

technical_breakdown.method: The paper introduces AWM-GRPO, which modifies the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) reward function to include a signal for 'memory-only answerability.' This ensures that trajectories are rewarded not just for correct final answers, but for maintaining a terminal working memory that is sufficient to answer the question independently of the original page images.
technical_breakdown.architecture: VLM Agent pipeline consisting of page retrieval, image inspection, working memory writing, and answer synthesis. The core innovation is the AWM diagnostic module that evaluates the terminal working memory.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) where the reward function is augmented to assign higher advantages to trajectories that are both answer-correct and have answerable terminal working memory. A diagnostic metric is used to measure if a reader can answer from the question and terminal memory alone.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Adds a diagnostic evaluation step to the training loop to compute memory-only answerability, likely increasing computational overhead during reward calculation compared to standard answer-only GRPO, but the specific complexity class is not detailed in the abstract.

paper.title: Cross-lingual Biography Enrichment via Claim Extraction and Alignment
paper.summary: English Wikipedia is often treated as the default encyclopedic source, yet non-English Wikipedia editions can contain richer locally grounded information for long-tail figures. We study cross-lingual biography enrichment: enriching an existing English biography with facts supported by a non-English biography about the same person. Focusing on women from non-English-speaking contexts, we introduce \textsc{CLAW-4L}, a benchmark consisting of 300 Wikipedia biography pairs linking an English biography with its French, Chinese or Azerbaijani counterpart, along with claim annotations and a fine-grained claim-pair relation corpus. We propose a claim-based enrichment framework that extracts English claims from both biographies, aligns them to identify enrichment evidence from the non-English biography, and rewrites the English biography using the selected claims. Our results show that non-English Wikipedia biographies provide valuable evidence for improving English biography coverage, while lower-resource settings remain challenging.

analysis.problem_statement: How to effectively enrich English Wikipedia biographies with unique, locally grounded facts from non-English counterparts, particularly for long-tail figures from non-English-speaking contexts.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Language bias and data scarcity in English-centric knowledge bases, specifically the under-representation of long-tail entities in non-English-speaking regions.
analysis.executive_summary: This work addresses the limitation of English Wikipedia as the default source of truth by leveraging non-English editions to recover missing or richer local context. It introduces a benchmark and a claim-based framework that bridges linguistic gaps to improve the factual coverage of English biographies, highlighting the potential of multilingual data for enhancing global representation in AI knowledge systems.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Improvement in English biography coverage via cross-lingual fact enrichment
key_metrics.baseline: Existing English Wikipedia biographies

technical_breakdown.method: A claim-based enrichment pipeline that extracts atomic claims from both English and non-English biographies, aligns them to identify novel evidence, and rewrites the English text using selected claims.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Three-stage framework: (1) Claim Extraction from both source languages, (2) Cross-lingual Claim Alignment to identify enrichment opportunities, (3) Biography Rewriting using aligned claims.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Utilizes the CLAW-4L benchmark (300 pairs across French, Chinese, Azerbaijani) with fine-grained claim-pair relation annotations to train and evaluate the alignment and rewriting components.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not specified in summary

paper.title: MLLMCLIP: Feature-Level Distillation of MLLM for Robust Vision-Language Representations
paper.summary: Pretrained vision-language models such as CLIP excel at zero-shot recognition but often fail at compositionality, particularly attribute-object and relational structures. Recent studies mitigate this issue by augmenting training with synthetic hard negatives generated by a cascade of large language models and text-to-image models, which incurs substantial pipeline overhead. We instead propose MLLMCLIP, a heterogeneous distillation framework that transfers multimodal knowledge directly from a generative Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) teacher into a discriminative CLIP student, bypassing synthetic data entirely. To bridge the architectural mismatch between the two paradigms, we introduce an attention-based per-layer token selection and a CKA-based distillation loss. Compared to prior CLIP-enhancement methods, MLLMCLIP achieves state-of-the-art compositional accuracy while delivering consistent gains on standard zero-shot classification and image-text retrieval, showing that feature-level distillation strengthens both compositional and general vision-language representation capability.

analysis.problem_statement: Pretrained vision-language models like CLIP lack compositional reasoning capabilities, particularly in handling attribute-object and relational structures, while existing solutions relying on synthetic data generation incur high computational overhead.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Computational overhead and pipeline complexity associated with generating synthetic hard negatives for training compositional vision-language models.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the limitation of discriminative models like CLIP in compositional tasks by proposing a direct knowledge distillation framework from generative MLLMs. By bypassing the need for synthetic data pipelines, it offers a more efficient path to enhancing zero-shot recognition and compositional accuracy, bridging the gap between generative and discriminative paradigms.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Compositional accuracy
key_metrics.metric_value: State-of-the-art (specific numerical values not provided in summary)
key_metrics.baseline: Prior CLIP-enhancement methods using synthetic hard negatives

technical_breakdown.method: Heterogeneous distillation transferring multimodal knowledge from a generative MLLM teacher to a discriminative CLIP student.
technical_breakdown.architecture: MLLM teacher model, CLIP student model, attention-based per-layer token selection module, and CKA-based distillation loss function.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses attention mechanisms to select tokens per layer to bridge architectural mismatches and employs Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) for the distillation loss.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Reduces pipeline overhead by eliminating synthetic data generation, though specific training time or FLOPs are not detailed in the summary.

paper.title: EgoArgus: Benchmarking VLMs as Situational Assistants for Modality-Grounded User Supports
paper.summary: VLMs are increasingly positioned as daily assistants that perceive first-person environments, follow user dialogue, and decide how to help. Existing egocentric benchmarks mainly evaluate visual understanding in isolation, leaving open whether models can arbitrate between visual evidence and user-provided language when the two are helpful, irrelevant, or conflicting. We introduce EgoArgus, a human-annotated dataset for evaluating egocentric assistants on understanding and decision tasks in five dialogue-video daily scenarios. Our results demonstrate that it is still challenging for current VLMs as reliable egocentric assistants, which requires identifying which modality is trustworthy and deciding when intervention is warranted. Deeper analysis also shows that existing modality bias mitigation methods are quite restricted to enhance performance, providing insights to aid practioners into the deployment of current VLMs as daily assistants.

analysis.problem_statement: Current egocentric benchmarks fail to evaluate whether Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can effectively arbitrate between conflicting or complementary visual and linguistic modalities to determine appropriate user assistance.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Modality conflict resolution and situational awareness in multimodal decision-making.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the gap in evaluating VLMs as reliable daily assistants by introducing a benchmark that tests their ability to weigh visual evidence against user dialogue in complex scenarios. It highlights that current models struggle with modality trustworthiness and intervention timing, indicating that existing bias mitigation techniques are insufficient for robust deployment in first-person environments.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Performance on understanding and decision tasks in five dialogue-video daily scenarios
key_metrics.baseline: Current VLMs and existing modality bias mitigation methods

technical_breakdown.method: Introduction of EgoArgus, a human-annotated dataset for evaluating egocentric assistants on understanding and decision tasks.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Benchmark framework covering five dialogue-video daily scenarios; evaluates VLMs on modality arbitration (visual vs. language).
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Human annotation of scenarios where visual and linguistic inputs are helpful, irrelevant, or conflicting; analysis of modality bias mitigation methods.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not specified in abstract

paper.title: PonsRAG: A Pons-Inspired RAG Bridging Cognitive Islands for Coordinated Long Narrative Reasoning
paper.summary: Long Narrative Reasoning is an essential capability for processing and reasoning over complex narratives. While retrieval-augmented generation provides a promising framework, existing methods still face two critical challenges: cognitive islanding and cross-layer evidence disconnection. To address these issues, we propose PonsRAG, a coordinated RAG framework inspired by the biological pons. PonsRAG consists of two key components: Triple-Layer Indexing, which organizes documents into a connected knowledge structure to bridge cognitive islands, and Coordinated Reasoning, which retrieves evidence across distinct layers and integrates cross-layer information into a unified context. We evaluate PonsRAG on four long-context narrative benchmarks, and experimental results show that it outperforms the strongest baseline, achieving a 11.56% relative improvement in average accuracy on multi-choice tasks.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) frameworks struggle with long narrative reasoning due to cognitive islanding and the disconnection of evidence across different semantic layers.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Long-context coherence and cross-layer evidence integration in retrieval-augmented systems.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the fragmentation of knowledge in long-form narrative processing by proposing a biologically inspired RAG framework. By structuring documents into a connected multi-layer hierarchy, it enables more coherent reasoning over complex narratives than flat retrieval methods.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Relative improvement in average accuracy on multi-choice tasks
key_metrics.baseline: Strongest baseline method

technical_breakdown.method: A coordinated RAG framework that organizes documents into a connected knowledge structure and retrieves/integrates evidence across distinct layers.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Two key components: Triple-Layer Indexing (for organizing documents) and Coordinated Reasoning (for cross-layer evidence integration).
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Inspired by the biological pons; uses a triple-layer indexing scheme to bridge cognitive islands and a mechanism to unify cross-layer information into a single context.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not specified in the provided metadata.

paper.title: Distance Is Not Enough: Forget-Retain Alignment Gap Predicts LLM Relearning Robustness
paper.summary: Machine unlearning aims to make a model forget specific data, yet unlearned LLMs often fail to stay unlearned: brief fine-tuning can revive removed knowledge. Existing robustness predictors rely on global weight-space displacement, but distance alone can be misleading when random or destructive updates collapse performance. We argue that relearning robustness depends on update structure: robust unlearning should affect forget-critical weights while sparing retain-critical ones. We introduce the Forget-Retain Alignment Gap (FRAG), a training-free predictor that scores an update's forget-retain alignment without running a relearning attack, and separates selective from dense updates more reliably than global distance. Building on the forget-critical, retain-sparing principle, Forget-Retain Pruning (FRP) improves relearning robustness. Our results suggest that weight selectivity better explains robustness than distance alone. Code is available at https://github.com/Yi1-Chen/FRAG.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing metrics for machine unlearning robustness, such as global weight-space distance, fail to accurately predict whether a model will retain unlearned knowledge after brief fine-tuning because they do not account for the structural alignment of updates with forget-critical versus retain-critical weights.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Evaluation and robustness of machine unlearning in Large Language Models (LLMs), specifically the inability of global displacement metrics to distinguish between effective selective unlearning and destructive updates that collapse performance.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses a critical gap in the reliability of machine unlearning by demonstrating that the structural alignment of weight updates, rather than their magnitude, determines relearning robustness. By introducing the Forget-Retain Alignment Gap (FRAG), it provides a training-free method to predict unlearning efficacy without executing costly relearning attacks, offering a more precise diagnostic tool for ensuring that unlearned knowledge remains suppressed.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Prediction accuracy of relearning robustness and separation of selective vs. dense updates
key_metrics.baseline: Global weight-space displacement metrics

technical_breakdown.method: The paper proposes FRAG, a training-free predictor that scores an update's alignment between forget-critical and retain-critical weights, and FRP (Forget-Retain Pruning), a method that leverages this principle to improve robustness by selectively pruning or updating weights.
technical_breakdown.architecture: No new model architecture is introduced; the work focuses on post-hoc analysis of weight updates and pruning strategies applied to existing LLMs.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: FRAG calculates an alignment gap without running relearning attacks, distinguishing selective updates from dense ones. FRP implements the forget-critical, retain-sparing principle to modify weights.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Training-free for the prediction phase (FRAG), implying low computational overhead for evaluation compared to methods requiring iterative fine-tuning or attack simulations.

paper.title: OmniPhys: A Unified Multimodal Benchmark for Physics Understanding and Generation from Chinese Educational Corpora
paper.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong abilities in solving diverse visual and textual reasoning tasks. However, their development in the physics domain is significantly hindered by the lack of a comprehensive benchmark. To fill this gap, we introduce OmniPhys, a large-scale benchmark for multimodal physics understanding and reasoning, covering middle school through university-level problems from Chinese Educational Corpora. OmniPhys consists of 15,246 questions and 19,850 images, accompanied by detailed annotations that support fine-grained analysis of reasoning processes and knowledge usage. Beyond conventional evaluation, OmniPhys is a benchmark that systematically evaluates multimodal outputs in the physics domain, including models' ability to generate structured physics diagrams, which constitute a fundamental component of authentic physics problem solving. Extensive evaluations reveal critical gaps in the capabilities of current MLLMs, especially in complex reasoning and visual generation. To address this, we release OmniPhys to serve as a foundational resource for advancing multimodal intelligence in physics and scientific domains. Codes and data are available at https://github.com/ECNU-RAIL/OmniPhys-EMNLP2026.

analysis.problem_statement: The lack of a comprehensive, large-scale benchmark for evaluating Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) on physics-specific understanding, reasoning, and visual generation tasks.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Evaluation gap in scientific domains, specifically the absence of standardized datasets to measure MLLM performance in physics reasoning and diagram generation.
analysis.executive_summary: OmniPhys addresses the critical shortage of domain-specific benchmarks for physics, providing a large-scale dataset derived from Chinese educational corpora. It uniquely evaluates not only textual reasoning but also the generation of structured physics diagrams, a fundamental aspect of authentic problem-solving that current MLLMs struggle with.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Dataset scale and coverage of physics problems and images
key_metrics.baseline: Existing multimodal benchmarks lacking comprehensive physics coverage

technical_breakdown.method: Construction of a unified multimodal benchmark using data from Chinese Educational Corpora, covering middle school to university levels, with detailed annotations for reasoning and knowledge usage.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Benchmark dataset structure supporting both understanding (reasoning) and generation (diagram creation) tasks.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Inclusion of fine-grained annotations for reasoning processes and systematic evaluation of structured physics diagram generation.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: N/A (Dataset/Benchmark paper)

paper.title: GGSS: Geodesic-Gated Spherical Steering for Inference-Time Debiasing of Generative Vision-Language Models
paper.summary: Generative vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used in human-centered settings, yet they can produce demographically biased outputs even when images differ only in controlled attributes such as perceived race or gender. However, existing inference-time debiasers were largely designed for static embeddings or CLIP-like models rather than generative VLMs. We propose GGSS---Geodesic-Gated Spherical Steering---a norm-preserving intervention that discovers a counterfactual bias subspace on the unit hypersphere, steers visual tokens along geodesic arcs, and uses an adaptive gate to focus correction on tokens that carry stronger demographic signal. We evaluate four generative VLMs against ten adapted inference-time debiasing baselines and prompt-based mitigation under a single operating-point protocol across categorical, pairwise, and occupation-gender bias tests, while also measuring general visual-language capability. GGSS achieves the lowest average bias on all four models, significant on three of four backbones under paired permutation tests, while preserving MMStar accuracy within +/- 0.6 p.p. of the unsteered baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/dukesun99/GGSS.

analysis.problem_statement: Generative vision-language models (VLMs) produce demographically biased outputs based on controlled attributes like race or gender, and existing inference-time debiasers are not designed for the generative nature of these models.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Algorithmic bias and fairness in generative AI outputs, specifically the lack of effective inference-time interventions for generative VLMs.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical gap in fairness mitigation for generative VLMs by introducing GGSS, a method that operates directly on the model's internal representations during inference. It is significant because it allows for real-time bias correction without retraining the model, ensuring that visual-language capabilities remain intact while reducing demographic biases.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Lowest average bias score across categorical, pairwise, and occupation-gender tests
key_metrics.metric_value: MMStar accuracy preserved within +/- 0.6 percentage points of baseline
key_metrics.baseline: Ten adapted inference-time debiasing baselines and prompt-based mitigation
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: Not explicitly quantified as a single percentage in the summary, but described as 'lowest average bias' and 'significant' under paired permutation tests.

technical_breakdown.method: GGSS is a norm-preserving intervention that identifies a counterfactual bias subspace on the unit hypersphere and steers visual tokens along geodesic arcs.
technical_breakdown.architecture: The system utilizes an adaptive gate to focus corrections on tokens with stronger demographic signals, applied to the visual token representations of generative VLMs.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: The method involves discovering a bias subspace on the unit hypersphere, performing geodesic steering of visual tokens, and applying an adaptive gating mechanism to modulate the strength of the intervention.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Inference-time intervention, implying no additional training cost but added computational overhead during the generation phase for subspace discovery and steering.

paper.title: GUIDE: Generative Unsupervised Chinese Query Correction via Phonetic and Visual Shared-ID Encoding
paper.summary: Chinese query correction (CQC) is important for search and query recommendation on content platforms, but supervised methods rely on large annotated correction pairs that are costly to maintain as query vocabularies evolve. Unsupervised correction with language models is attractive, yet in the short-query setting, unconstrained generation often over-corrects ambiguous inputs toward high-frequency phrases, causing intent drift. We propose \textsc{GUIDE}, a generative unsupervised framework for CQC based on a confuse-then-clarify paradigm. \textsc{GUIDE} encodes phonetically or visually confusable characters with shared-IDs and reconstructs the original query with an encoder--decoder architecture, which constrains correction to plausible confusion neighborhoods while learning from unlabeled query streams. A time-decayed, query-frequency-weighted objective further supports adaptation to rapidly changing query vocabularies. Experiments on \textit{QSpell 250K} and a large-scale real-world dataset (\textit{KwaiSearch}) show that \textsc{GUIDE} consistently outperforms strong baselines, while online A/B testing further confirms gains in correction quality and downstream engagement.
paper.comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Industry Track; 7 pages, 3 figures, 8 tables

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the challenge of performing accurate Chinese query correction in short-query settings without relying on costly annotated data, specifically preventing the over-correction and intent drift common in unconstrained generative models.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Data scarcity and annotation cost for supervised learning, as well as the semantic drift (over-correction) inherent in unsupervised generative models for low-resource or short-text tasks.
analysis.executive_summary: GUIDE offers a scalable, unsupervised solution for Chinese query correction that eliminates the need for large-scale manual annotation, which is critical for maintaining search relevance in dynamic content platforms. By constraining generation to phonetic and visual confusion neighborhoods, it mitigates the risk of altering user intent, a common failure mode in LLM-based correction. The framework's ability to adapt to rapidly changing query vocabularies via time-decayed weighting makes it highly relevant for real-time industrial search systems.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Consistent outperformance of strong baselines in correction quality and downstream engagement.
key_metrics.baseline: Strong supervised and unsupervised baselines (specific names not listed in summary)

technical_breakdown.method: A 'confuse-then-clarify' generative framework that encodes confusable characters with shared IDs to constrain the search space, followed by reconstruction using an encoder-decoder model trained on unlabeled data.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Encoder-decoder architecture with a specialized input encoding layer that maps phonetically or visually similar characters to shared identifiers.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses a time-decayed, query-frequency-weighted objective function to handle evolving vocabularies; employs shared-ID encoding for phonetic/visual confusables to limit correction to plausible neighborhoods.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not explicitly stated, but implies standard encoder-decoder training overhead with additional logic for dynamic ID mapping and frequency weighting.
