paper.title: Dynamic Haven Selection for Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery in Constrained Warehouses
paper.summary: Space-efficient warehouse layouts often contain single-agent-width aisles and dead-end workstations where robots have few places to wait without blocking others. In Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery (MAPD) on such constrained layouts, robots must accept online pickup-delivery tasks while preserving protected waiting locations called Havens. The Safe HAven Retreat Planner (SHARP) introduced a mechanism that extends each committed task path with a validated retreat to the agent's dedicated initial Haven, but fixed-Haven commitments can send agents toward distant Havens after deliveries. We present A-sharp (Adaptive SHARP), which changes an agent's retreat target at task assignment time. A naive switch can cause two agents to rely on the same waiting location or let another committed path pass through a location that is still occupied or reserved. A-sharp prevents these failures with an availability test for candidate Havens and a pending-release rule that keeps the previous Haven protected until the agent departs. Under explicit Haven-structure and Safe Interval Path Planning (SIPP) assumptions, we prove invariant preservation and finite-release completeness: every task in any finite release sequence is delivered in finite time. Across 72,000 runs on 14,400 paired map-agent-count-rate-seed cases over four maps, both SHARP and A-sharp complete their respective 14,400 runs. For makespan (final delivery time), a prespecified paired comparison with Holm correction over all 138 configurations with more Havens than agents finds A-sharp significantly better in 107 configurations and never significantly worse than SHARP; on the tested tree map, the median reduction is 16.7%.
paper.comment: 19 pages, 4 figures, and 3 tables. Accepted at the Joint Workshop on Planning for Complex Real-World Applications (CAIPI) and Bridging the Gap Between AI Planning and (Reinforcement) Learning (PRL), co-located with IJCAI-ECAI 2026

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the challenge of preventing deadlocks and blocking in multi-agent pickup and delivery (MAPD) within space-constrained warehouse layouts by dynamically selecting safe waiting locations (Havens) for agents.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Inefficiency and potential deadlock in multi-agent path planning due to static resource allocation (fixed Havens) in constrained environments.
analysis.executive_summary: This work improves the efficiency of autonomous warehouse logistics by enabling agents to adaptively select optimal waiting spots rather than relying on fixed initial locations. By proving finite-release completeness and demonstrating significant makespan reductions, it offers a robust solution for dense, real-world robotic operations where space is limited.

key_metrics.baseline: SHARP (Safe HAven Retreat Planner) with fixed-Haven commitments.

technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Utilizes an availability test to prevent multiple agents from relying on the same waiting location and a pending-release rule to maintain invariant preservation, ensuring no committed path passes through occupied or reserved locations.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: The paper proves finite-release completeness, indicating that every task in a finite sequence is delivered in finite time, though specific computational complexity bounds (e.g., Big-O) are not explicitly detailed in the summary.

paper.title: Decoupling Planning and Control for Instructable Agents
paper.summary: Recent work shows that pre-trained, instruction-tuned vision-language models (VLMs) perform well at mapping from instructions and observations to high-level plans, but struggle to realize such plans as reliable low-latency action sequences in unfamiliar environments. At the same time, world-model controllers excel at fast observation-to-action control, but lack open-ended task guidance. In this work, we combine these strengths into a single system, Instruct-to-Act, where we train a world-model controller to act autonomously at high frequency when conditioned on sparse, higher-latency, and high-level text instructions generated by a VLM planner. To train controllers to be language-instructable, we relabel segments of controller policy rollouts with synthetic instructions and jointly optimize a behavior-cloning objective along with existing reward-maximizing and world-modeling objectives. We evaluate our proposed approach across seven embodied environments, including three multi-agent environments where VLM planners coordinate through language while trained controllers serve as their actuators. Under matched observation and action spaces, our decoupled approach consistently outperforms controller-only and direct VLM action-generation variants, preserves fast control, and lets us swap in different pretrained VLM planners without fine-tuning, while remaining competitive with strong vision-language-action and multi-agent RL baselines on six of seven tasks.

analysis.executive_summary: This work bridges the disconnect between semantic understanding and physical execution by decoupling planning and control. It enables robust, real-time embodied agents that can be guided by diverse, pre-trained VLMs without requiring fine-tuning of the controller for each new planner.

technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Requires joint optimization of multiple objectives (behavior cloning, reward, world modeling) and evaluation across seven environments, including three multi-agent settings.

paper.title: Towards Expert Financial QA via Self-Improving RAG
paper.summary: Expert-level financial question answering requires both grounded verification to catch numeric hallucinations and audit trails for regulatory compliance, attributes that standard single-pass RAG systems lack. We take a step toward this goal with Self-Improving RAG, a framework that decomposes document QA into three specialized agents (Retrieval, Reasoning, and Judge) coordinated by an orchestrator with feedback-driven self-correction. When the Judge Agent scores an answer below a dynamic threshold, the system triggers retry with escalated strategies: broader retrieval, more careful prompting, and relaxed acceptance criteria. We evaluate on FinanceBench (SEC filing QA), where Self-Improving RAG achieves 86% oracle-guided accuracy (measuring agreement with gold answers) with a 36.4% Lazarus Rate, recovering nearly 4 in 10 initially incorrect answers through targeted retry. A key finding is that a fixed retrieval pipeline with judge-driven retry achieves strong results without dynamic routing, providing full interpretability. Every decision is logged with confidence scores, enabling the audit trails required for regulated financial applications.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper introduces a multi-agent RAG framework that enhances financial QA accuracy by incorporating a judge-driven self-correction loop, which recovers a significant portion of initially incorrect answers. It demonstrates that a fixed retrieval pipeline with dynamic retry strategies can achieve high accuracy while maintaining full interpretability, a critical requirement for regulated financial applications.

paper.title: FOCUS & RePAIR: Mitigating Text Degeneration via Token-Level Guidance for Pruned Large Language Models
paper.summary: Pruning is a practical approach to compress large language models (LLMs), but it can amplify text degeneration, especially repetition loops, even when perplexity and task accuracy remain largely unchanged. In this work, we present a token-level analysis of this failure mode by viewing decoding as a dynamical process that enters and persists in a small set of recurrent contexts. Our analysis decomposes degeneration into loop entry risk and loop persistence, and shows that persistence is controlled by the escape mass assigned to plausible alternatives within the token sampling set. Motivated by these findings, we propose two token-level guidance objectives for post-pruning fine-tuning. FOCUS reweights distillation toward high-confidence teacher regions to suppress leakage, while RePAIR uses onset-centered positive/negative continuation pairs with a margin loss to promote plausible alternatives and prevent early commitment to repetition loops. Experiments on open-ended continuation and instruction-based generation show that both methods consistently reduce repetition and improve generation quality.

By analyzing decoding as a dynamical process, it provides targeted fine-tuning strategies to restore generation diversity and quality in compressed models.

paper.title: FU-Mamba: A Frequency-Enhanced Dynamic Scanning Framework for Oralscan Image Segmentation
paper.summary: Oralscan image segmentation is essential for computer-aided diagnosis and treatment planning in digital dentistry. However, existing visual state space models (SSMs) often rely on manually designed scanning orders to flatten image patches into sequences, which disrupts the semantic spatial continuity and hinders coherent feature extraction from key foreground regions. Moreover, elements such as inconsistent lighting, reflective surfaces, and noise during data acquisition disrupt the frequency distribution by diminishing high-frequency details while enhancing low-frequency components, consequently hindering the accurate localization of boundaries. In response to these challenges, we introduce FU-Mamba, an innovative framework that incorporates dynamic scanning and frequency domain enhancement within the SSM architecture. Specifically, the Dynamic Mamba Block (DMB) adaptively learns sampling offsets via a trainable offset prediction network and performs flexible bilinear interpolation, enabling content-aware scanning that preserves spatial coherence. Furthermore, a frequency domain enhancement block balances spectral components through wavelet-guided decomposition and spectrum pooling, improving robustness under adverse imaging conditions. Experimental findings indicate that FU-Mamba attains a notable enhancement in segmentation accuracy, evidenced by a 1.1% increase in the mean intersection over union (mIoU) metric when evaluated on the dental segmentation dataset. Project page: https://byte2bite.github.io/FU-Mamba/

analysis.problem_statement: Existing visual State Space Models (SSMs) for oralscan image segmentation suffer from disrupted spatial continuity due to fixed scanning orders and reduced boundary localization accuracy caused by frequency distortions from lighting and noise.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Spatial coherence in sequence modeling and robustness to frequency domain artifacts in medical imaging.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the limitations of standard Mamba architectures in dental imaging by introducing content-aware scanning and frequency enhancement. It is relevant to the AI landscape as it demonstrates how integrating domain-specific signal processing (wavelets) and adaptive spatial sampling can improve segmentation precision in noisy, specialized medical datasets.

The DMB uses a trainable offset prediction network to generate sampling offsets, while the enhancement block uses wavelet-guided decomposition to mitigate low-frequency dominance and high-frequency loss.

paper.title: HOLMES: In-Context Failure-Center Localization for High-Dimensional Yield Estimation
paper.summary: Importance sampling for high-sigma yield estimation requires locating the failure center from a severely imbalanced sample set. Existing surrogate-assisted methods rely on iterative gradient-based training, ill-posed under extreme class imbalance; model errors propagate into the estimator, causing accuracy collapse in high dimensions. We recast failure-center localization as few-shot binary classification: a prior-fitted tabular foundation model performs gradient-free in-context inference in a single forward pass, eliminating the ill-posed training loop. \textbf{HOLMES} (High-sigma Optimal Localization via Manifold Estimation and Sampling) pairs this with an SVD-based anisotropic proposal that captures the local geometry of the failure manifold, and a hit-rate-driven adaptive mixing scheme that stabilizes importance weights where conventional adaptation collapses. On 6T SRAM benchmarks spanning $D = 108$ to $D = 1{,}152$, full-dimensional baselines exhibit accuracy collapse at some dimension, with the strongest baseline reaching 25.8\% relative error; PCA+MNIS is additionally evaluated at the two largest dimensions. HOLMES remains within 5.9\% across all five configurations with up to $58.8\times$ speedup over Monte Carlo. The code is available on \href{https://github.com/IceLab-JCIE/ICE006-Yield-Holmes}

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the challenge of accurately locating the failure center in high-dimensional spaces for high-sigma yield estimation, where existing surrogate-assisted methods suffer from ill-posed training and accuracy collapse due to extreme class imbalance.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: This addresses the bottleneck of model instability and accuracy degradation in few-shot learning scenarios characterized by extreme class imbalance and high dimensionality, specifically within the context of statistical yield analysis.
analysis.executive_summary: HOLMES recasts failure-center localization as a few-shot binary classification problem, utilizing a pre-trained tabular foundation model to perform gradient-free in-context inference, thereby eliminating the unstable iterative training loop. By combining this with an SVD-based anisotropic proposal and adaptive mixing, the method achieves robust performance in high-dimensional settings where conventional baselines fail, offering significant speedups over Monte Carlo simulations.

key_metrics.baseline: Full-dimensional baselines (strongest baseline reached 25.8% relative error) and Monte Carlo

technical_breakdown.architecture: Components include a tabular foundation model for few-shot classification, an SVD-based module for anisotropic proposal generation, and an adaptive mixing controller for importance sampling weights.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Utilizes in-context learning (single forward pass) instead of iterative gradient-based training; employs Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to model local geometry; applies hit-rate-driven adaptation to prevent weight collapse.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Achieves up to 58.8x speedup over Monte Carlo; eliminates iterative training loops, reducing computational overhead associated with surrogate model training.

paper.title: Unsupervised Adaptation of 3D CT Foundation Models for 3D CBCT Segmentation
paper.summary: Accurate 3D segmentation of cone-beam CT (CBCT) is critical for interventional and radiation therapy applications, yet it remains limited by two compounding challenges: the scarcity of annotated CBCT data and the large domain shift from diagnostic CT. Interventional CBCT exhibits fundamental modality differences from conventional CT, driven by acquisition and physics effects as well as contrast-specific vascular content, thereby limiting effective cross-modality model transfer. We propose a novel unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) framework based on redundancy-reducing feature alignment, enabling 3D CBCT segmentation with no target-domain annotations or inference-time adaptation. Our framework is architecture-agnostic, seamlessly adapting both CNN-based and ViT-based foundation models. We evaluate our method on two challenging CT-CBCT liver segmentation benchmarks: one for interventional vascular procedures and one for radiation therapy, demonstrating that even large-scale pretrained segmentation networks require explicit feature-space bridging to generalize across acquisition modalities, and that our approach consistently outperforms existing pretrained foundation model and UDA strategies. To support reproducibility and benchmarking, we release the liver segmentations for a public CBCT dataset, along with the code, trained models, and weights.
paper.comment: Accepted at the EMA4MICCAI workshop at MICCAI 2026. 11 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Code, trained models, weights, and liver annotations are available at https://github.com/mirabll/FARR3D/

analysis.executive_summary: This work is significant because it demonstrates that large-scale pretrained foundation models, despite their general capabilities, fail to generalize across acquisition modalities without explicit feature-space alignment. By introducing an unsupervised domain adaptation framework that requires no target-domain annotations, it enables the deployment of advanced 3D segmentation models in resource-constrained interventional and radiation therapy settings.

paper.title: Parameter-Efficient pretrained-CT-to-MRI Transfer for Rectal Cancer Segmentation: Performance-Calibration Trade-offs
paper.summary: Accurate rectal cancer segmentation from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is essential for adaptive radiotherapy and tumor response assessment, but deployment also requires computational efficiency and informative, calibrated uncertainty estimates. We therefore introduce SWIFT, a SWin pretrained model wIth parameter-eFficient and Tumor-aware fine-tuning for rectal cancer segmentation. A Swin V2 encoder pretrained on 10,444 public 3D CT volumes using a DINOv2-style objective was adapted to T2-weighted MRI through four cumulative configurations: full fine-tuning (SWIFT), decoder compression (SWIFTe), low-rank adaptation (SWIFTe-LoRA), and a four-member LoRA-decoder ensemble (SWIFTe-LDE4). Geometric accuracy, tumor detection, radiomic agreement, and probability calibration were evaluated on a held-out 247-case test set from a single-institution cohort acquired using 1.5 or 3 Tesla GE scanners. Compared with SWIFT, SWIFTe reduced total parameters by 70.1% (from 72.8M to 21.8M) and increased tumor detection rate from 89.9% to 93.9%, while achieving a slightly lower median surface DSC (0.61 versus 0.62) and improved radiomic agreement. In a separate SWIFTe ablation, removing tumor-aware augmentation reduced detection from 93.9% to 89.9% but increased surface DSC from 0.61 to 0.64, demonstrating a detection-boundary-agreement trade-off. SWIFTe-LoRA used 14.6% of SWIFTe's trainable parameters while retaining similar segmentation performance. SWIFTe-LDE4 achieved the lowest calibration errors among the four configurations after temperature scaling (expected calibration error, 0.217; Brier score, 0.222), although the absolute expected calibration error indicates residual miscalibration. Similar efficiency-calibration patterns were observed using the public VoCo checkpoint, supporting robustness across pretrained initializations rather than external clinical generalizability.

analysis.problem_statement: How to efficiently adapt a large-scale CT-pretrained model for accurate and calibrated rectal cancer segmentation on T2-weighted MRI without incurring the high computational costs of full fine-tuning.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: High computational cost and parameter inefficiency of full fine-tuning large vision transformers for medical image segmentation, alongside the challenge of achieving calibrated uncertainty estimates in domain-shifted scenarios (CT to MRI).
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the trade-off between model efficiency, segmentation accuracy, and uncertainty calibration when transferring knowledge from CT to MRI for rectal cancer. By introducing SWIFT, it demonstrates that parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) strategies like LoRA and decoder compression can maintain or even improve tumor detection rates while significantly reducing model size. The work highlights that while efficiency and calibration can be optimized, there is a distinct trade-off between tumor detection sensitivity and boundary agreement (DSC).

key_metrics.primary_metric: Reduction in total parameters while maintaining/improving tumor detection rate
key_metrics.metric_value: 70.1% parameter reduction (72.8M to 21.8M); Tumor detection rate increased from 89.9% to 93.9%
key_metrics.baseline: SWIFT (Full fine-tuning of Swin V2 encoder)
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: 70.1% reduction in parameters; 4.0% absolute increase in tumor detection rate

technical_breakdown.method: Adapting a Swin V2 encoder pretrained on 3D CT volumes (using DINOv2-style objective) to T2-weighted MRI via cumulative configurations: full fine-tuning, decoder compression, low-rank adaptation (LoRA), and LoRA-decoder ensemble.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Swin V2 encoder (pretrained on 10,444 CT volumes) with a segmentation decoder. Variants include compressed decoders (SWIFTe), LoRA adapters (SWIFTe-LoRA), and an ensemble of four LoRA-decoder members (SWIFTe-LDE4).
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses DINOv2-style self-supervised pretraining on CT. Fine-tuning involves tumor-aware augmentation. Evaluation includes geometric accuracy (Surface DSC), tumor detection rate, radiomic agreement, and probability calibration (Expected Calibration Error, Brier score) after temperature scaling.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Significantly reduced trainable parameters (SWIFTe-LoRA uses 14.6% of SWIFTe's trainable parameters). Lower computational overhead for inference and fine-tuning compared to full fine-tuning, though ensemble methods (LDE4) may increase inference latency.

paper.title: CorporateBench: Large-Scale Q&A Benchmarking with Temporal Knowledge Bases
paper.summary: LLMs are increasingly able to answer complex questions about enterprise-scale document collections. But evaluation is hard: companies don't want to share internal communications, and synthetic datasets have been overly simple. We present CorporateBench (CB), a human-validated multi-task Q&A benchmark whose scale approaches the conditions LLMs encounter in corporate communication networks, with evaluation corpora surpassing 230,000 documents. CB evaluates LLMs across two dimensions (information extraction and knowledge base querying) through four synthetically generated firms ranging from 12 to 10,000 employees. Each corpus is sampled from a temporally evolving knowledge base describing a consistent world, guaranteeing cross-document logical consistency even across hundreds of thousands of documents. We evaluate five LLMs on CB, revealing increasingly poor performance as input size approaches realistic scales. CB provides LLM developers a metric for corporate communication reasoning, filling a crucial gap in the benchmarking ecosystem.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing benchmarks for evaluating Large Language Models on enterprise-scale document collections are limited by the privacy constraints of real corporate data and the oversimplification of synthetic datasets, failing to capture the complexity and scale of real-world corporate communication networks.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Evaluation and Benchmarking
analysis.executive_summary: This paper introduces CorporateBench, a large-scale, human-validated Q&A benchmark designed to test LLMs on enterprise document collections of up to 230,000 documents. It addresses the gap between synthetic data simplicity and real-world corporate data privacy by using temporally evolving, logically consistent synthetic firms. The results demonstrate that current LLMs suffer significant performance degradation as input scales approach realistic corporate sizes.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Performance degradation of LLMs on Q&A tasks as input document scale increases
key_metrics.metric_value: Corpora size up to 230,000 documents; 4 synthetic firms (12-10,000 employees)
key_metrics.baseline: Five evaluated LLMs compared against each other across varying input scales
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: N/A (Benchmark paper, not a model improvement paper)

technical_breakdown.method: Generation of four synthetic firms with temporally evolving knowledge bases to ensure cross-document logical consistency, followed by human validation of multi-task Q&A pairs covering information extraction and knowledge base querying.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Temporal Knowledge Base (TKB) framework generating consistent world states across time; evaluation pipeline spanning two dimensions (IE and KB querying) across four firm scales.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Synthetic data generation ensuring logical consistency across hundreds of thousands of documents; human validation process for Q&A pairs; evaluation of five specific LLMs.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: N/A (Focus is on benchmark construction and evaluation, not model training complexity)

paper.title: D2C-Routing: Dimension-to-Composition Evidence Routing for Mixed-Origin AI-Generated Text Detection
paper.summary: AI-generated text detection is commonly framed as a binary document-level judgment about whether a text is human-written or machine-generated. This framing breaks down for mixed-origin writing, where content origin and expression origin may differ. We cast mixed-origin detection as dimension-to-composition source attribution, inferring content origin and expression origin before composing them into four collaboration types. We propose Dimension-to-Composition Routing (D2C-Routing), which routes content-side and expression-side evidence to supervised dimension heads before a learned gated composition layer predicts the final label. On MixD2C, a reconstructed split derived from the HART mixed-origin benchmark, our disclosed D2C-Routing-based detector system reaches 0.8603 four-way Avg TPR@1%FPR, 6.5 points above the same-split RACE-local rerun. Core ablations support the routing design, while error analysis shows that distinguishing AI-content/human-expression from fully AI-generated text remains the hardest boundary. Code is available at https://github.com/bystander563/d2c-routing-artifact.
paper.comment: 17 pages, 4 figures. To appear in EMNLP 2026

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the failure of standard binary AI-generated text detection methods in mixed-origin scenarios where the content source and expression source differ.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: It addresses the bottleneck of coarse-grained binary classification that fails to distinguish between different types of human-AI collaboration (e.g., AI content with human editing vs. fully AI-generated).
analysis.executive_summary: As AI tools increasingly assist in writing, the binary human-vs-machine distinction becomes obsolete, requiring systems that can attribute specific dimensions of text to their origins. This work provides a structured framework for detecting these nuanced collaboration types, which is critical for academic integrity and content provenance in the era of generative AI.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Four-way Average True Positive Rate at 1% False Positive Rate (Avg TPR@1%FPR)
key_metrics.baseline: RACE-local rerun on the same MixD2C split

technical_breakdown.method: The approach casts detection as dimension-to-composition source attribution, first inferring content and expression origins separately before combining them to predict one of four collaboration types.
technical_breakdown.architecture: The D2C-Routing architecture consists of supervised dimension heads for content-side and expression-side evidence, followed by a learned gated composition layer that predicts the final label.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: The system routes specific evidence types to dedicated heads and uses a gating mechanism in the composition layer to integrate these signals. It is evaluated on MixD2C, a reconstructed split from the HART benchmark.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not specified in the provided metadata.

paper.title: DataKernelBench: Can LLMs Optimize Database Queries on GPUs?
paper.summary: GPUs increasingly accelerate database systems, but query-specific peak performance still often relies on hand-written kernels. Existing LLM kernel benchmarks focus on machine learning operators, leaving irregular, heterogeneous, data-movement-heavy database-style operators untested. We introduce DataKernelBench, which translates SQL into validated PyTorch TorchPlan programs and evaluates LLMs that optimize either the core tensor-bounded snippet or the full query in CUDA or Triton through execution-guided repair. Across ten proprietary and open-weight models on TPC-H SF10 with an H100 GPU, the strongest full-query CUDA configuration achieves $2.11\times$ speedup over the TorchPlan baseline at full pass rate. We find that higher-performing implementations commonly use kernel fusion and execution-strategy changes, stronger models benefit most from full-query specialization, and workload context matters more than hardware context. To handle data larger than GPU memory, we extend TorchPlan with Dask-cuDF for on-demand partition loading on TPC-H SF100 with four H100 GPUs, achieving $2.54\times$ speedup.   Project page: https://kerneldf.github.io/datakernelbench

analysis.problem_statement: Existing LLM kernel benchmarks fail to evaluate the ability of large language models to optimize irregular, data-movement-heavy database operators on GPUs, which currently rely on hand-written kernels for peak performance.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: The lack of automated, high-performance kernel generation for heterogeneous and irregular database workloads, which limits the scalability and efficiency of GPU-accelerated database systems.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper introduces DataKernelBench, a benchmark that bridges the gap between ML-focused kernel optimization and complex database query execution by translating SQL into PyTorch TorchPlan programs. It demonstrates that LLMs can significantly outperform baseline tensor operations through execution-guided repair, highlighting the potential for AI-driven optimization in data-intensive systems beyond standard machine learning operators.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Speedup over TorchPlan baseline
key_metrics.baseline: TorchPlan baseline (full pass rate)

technical_breakdown.method: The system translates SQL queries into validated PyTorch TorchPlan programs and evaluates LLMs that generate optimized CUDA or Triton kernels for either core tensor snippets or full queries, using an execution-guided repair loop to fix errors.
technical_breakdown.architecture: The architecture consists of a SQL-to-TorchPlan translation layer, an LLM-based kernel generation module, and an execution environment on H100 GPUs. For out-of-memory scenarios, it extends TorchPlan with Dask-cuDF for on-demand partition loading across multiple GPUs.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Key techniques include kernel fusion, execution-strategy changes, and full-query specialization. The benchmark utilizes TPC-H SF10 and SF100 datasets, with the SF100 configuration leveraging four H100 GPUs and Dask-cuDF for distributed memory management.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: The approach relies on iterative LLM inference and execution feedback rather than traditional training, with computational costs dominated by the GPU execution of generated kernels and the LLM inference time for repair cycles.

paper.title: BALMS: Benchmarking Agentic LLMs for Longitudinal Mental Health Sensing
paper.summary: Mental health assessment relies on episodic self-report scales, which convert subjective states such as stress into numerical scores but provide only sparse snapshots of wellbeing. Wearable devices offer longitudinal behavioral and physiological signals for continuous, low-burden monitoring. Recent LLM-driven personal-health agents enable natural language queries over wearable signals, but mainly handle short-term, retrieval-based lookups (e.g., highest step count over a week). They do not evaluate whether agents can reason over long-term signals to predict wellbeing scores paired with evidence-grounded rationales. To address this gap, we introduce BALMS, the first systematic benchmark of LLM-based agentic systems for longitudinal mental health sensing. BALMS spans 3 real-world longitudinal datasets, 2 task families (closed-form wellbeing-score prediction and rationale generation auto-graded by an LLM-as-Judge), 3 agentic paradigms evaluated across 5 open- and closed-source LLM backbones. We find that zero-shot agents rarely outperform a simple mean baseline, except with stronger backbones or compact, semantically meaningful features. Chain-of-thought prompting improves reasoning-oriented backbones, but does not guarantee temporal grounding or numerical correctness. Together with more analysis on efficiency and temporal scaling, BALMS highlights the need for longitudinal mental health agents that selectively retrieve history, ground temporal evidence, and reason over interpretable behavioral features.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing LLM-driven personal health agents lack the capability to reason over long-term longitudinal wearable signals to predict wellbeing scores with evidence-grounded rationales, relying instead on short-term retrieval-based lookups.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Temporal reasoning and long-horizon context integration in agentic LLM systems for continuous health monitoring.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper introduces BALMS, the first systematic benchmark for evaluating LLM-based agentic systems on longitudinal mental health sensing. It highlights that current zero-shot agents often fail to outperform simple baselines in temporal reasoning and numerical correctness, despite improvements from chain-of-thought prompting, thereby identifying critical gaps in grounding temporal evidence for interpretable health predictions.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Comparison of agentic LLM performance against simple baselines in closed-form wellbeing-score prediction and rationale generation.
key_metrics.metric_value: Not explicitly quantified in summary; qualitative finding that zero-shot agents rarely outperform mean baseline.
key_metrics.baseline: Simple mean baseline for wellbeing-score prediction.
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: Not provided in summary; noted as generally negative or marginal for zero-shot agents without strong backbones or compact features.

technical_breakdown.method: Systematic benchmarking of 3 agentic paradigms across 5 LLM backbones using 3 real-world longitudinal datasets, evaluating both closed-form score prediction and LLM-as-Judge graded rationale generation.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Agentic LLM systems processing longitudinal behavioral and physiological signals from wearable devices, utilizing retrieval mechanisms and chain-of-thought prompting strategies.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Evaluation across open- and closed-source LLM backbones, analysis of efficiency and temporal scaling, and testing of compact, semantically meaningful features versus raw signal retrieval.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Focuses on inference-time complexity and temporal scaling efficiency rather than training overhead, highlighting the need for selective history retrieval to manage long-context costs.

paper.title: PACE: A Unified Condense-and-Extract Paradigm for Fast VLM Inference
paper.summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) demonstrate exceptional visual reasoning capabilities, yet their inference costs escalate rapidly with the proliferation of visual tokens. Existing visual token pruning methods exhibit two fundamental limitations. First, most approaches operate exclusively post-vision encoder, leaving the substantial latency of the visual encoding phase unoptimized. Second, under strict token budgets, these methods often fail to jointly preserve holistic visual contexts and fine-grained details, leading to performance degradation. To address these bottlenecks, we propose PACE (Pixel-Adaptive Condense and Extract), a training-free inference framework that accelerates both the vision encoder and the Large Language Model (LLM) via a unified Condense-and-Extract paradigm. During the Condense stage, an Adaptive Pixel Compressor (APC) evaluates visual information density prior to encoding, adaptively downsampling redundant inputs, curtailing encoder computation while preserving global context and essential visual cues. In the Extract stage, a Dynamic Dual-Attention Extractor (DDAE) selectively retains visual tokens via a fusion of internal visual signals from the encoder and semantic signals from the LLM, safeguarding task-critical details. By integrating PACE into Qwen2.5-VL-7B, the model retains 93.8% of its original performance while utilizing only 10% of the visual tokens, yielding a 3.1x speedup in time to first token (TTFT). Our code is available at https://github.com/jjL357/PACE.
paper.comment: 22 pages, 9 figures, 13 tables. Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026

analysis.problem_statement: Vision-Language Models suffer from high inference latency and performance degradation when using existing visual token pruning methods that fail to optimize the vision encoder phase or jointly preserve holistic context and fine-grained details under strict token budgets.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Inference latency and computational cost associated with processing large volumes of visual tokens in VLMs.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical scalability issue of VLM inference by optimizing both the vision encoder and LLM stages simultaneously. By reducing visual tokens to 10% of the original count while retaining over 93% of performance, it enables significantly faster deployment of high-capacity multimodal models without requiring retraining.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Performance retention and Time to First Token (TTFT) speedup
key_metrics.metric_value: 93.8% performance retention, 3.1x TTFT speedup, 10% visual token usage
key_metrics.baseline: Qwen2.5-VL-7B (original full-token inference)

technical_breakdown.method: A training-free, unified Condense-and-Extract paradigm that adaptively downsamples inputs before encoding and selectively retains tokens after encoding based on fused attention signals.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Two-stage pipeline: 1) Adaptive Pixel Compressor (APC) for pre-encoding density evaluation and downsampling; 2) Dynamic Dual-Attention Extractor (DDAE) for post-encoding token selection.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: APC evaluates visual information density to curtail encoder computation; DDAE fuses internal visual signals from the encoder and semantic signals from the LLM to identify task-critical tokens.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Training-free inference framework; reduces computational load by processing only 10% of visual tokens, yielding a 3.1x reduction in Time to First Token.

paper.title: Ancient-Bench: A Comprehensive Multi-millennial, Multi-medium, and Multi-script Benchmark for Ancient Chinese Artifact Text Recognition
paper.summary: Ancient Chinese artifact text recognition is fundamental to heritage digitization, and benchmarks for ancient texts are essential for evaluating current model capabilities. However, existing benchmarks suffer from ''fragmentation'', manifested in limited temporal coverage, limited medium diversity, and incomplete script types. Therefore, we present Ancient-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark of 2,700 images for ancient Chinese artifact text recognition, featuring three dimensions: Multi-millennial (spanning 3,000 years of character evolution), Multi-medium (covering nine artifact categories), and Multi-script (encompassing seven historical script forms). To enable consistent and fair evaluation across heterogeneous media, we further define three annotation standards tailored to the medium-specific characteristics of ancient texts: symbol standardization, character standardization, and parsing standardization. Extensive experiments on Ancient-Bench covering general Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and OCR-specialist models reveal that ancient Chinese artifact text recognition remains fundamentally unsolved, with persistent challenges in variant characters, specialized symbols, and hallucination. The dataset is available at https://github.com/SCUT-DLVCLab/Ancient_Bench.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing benchmarks for ancient Chinese artifact text recognition are fragmented, lacking sufficient coverage across temporal periods, artifact media, and historical script variations to provide a fair evaluation of model capabilities.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Data fragmentation and lack of comprehensive, standardized evaluation benchmarks for specialized, low-resource historical text recognition tasks.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical gap in heritage digitization by providing a unified, large-scale benchmark that spans 3,000 years of Chinese history, nine artifact types, and seven script forms. It establishes standardized annotation protocols to ensure fair comparison across heterogeneous media, revealing that current Vision-Language Models and OCR specialists still fail to robustly handle variant characters and specialized symbols.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Demonstration of persistent failure rates in variant character recognition and hallucination across state-of-the-art models.
key_metrics.metric_value: 2,700 images (dataset size); 3,000 years (temporal span); 9 media types; 7 script forms.
key_metrics.baseline: General Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and OCR-specialist models.
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: N/A (This is a benchmark paper, not a model improvement paper; it quantifies the gap rather than closing it.)

technical_breakdown.method: Construction of a multi-dimensional dataset with tailored annotation standards (symbol, character, and parsing standardization) to normalize evaluation across diverse ancient media.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Benchmark framework comprising 2,700 annotated images categorized by millennium, medium (9 categories), and script (7 forms), paired with an evaluation protocol for VLMs and OCR models.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Defines three specific annotation standards: symbol standardization for non-character glyphs, character standardization for variant forms, and parsing standardization for layout/structure. Experiments evaluate general VLMs and specialized OCR models against these standards.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: N/A (Dataset and benchmark release; computational complexity depends on the specific models evaluated, which are external to this contribution.)

paper.title: STAR : Sentence Translation Alignment Rate for Document-to-Document Machine Translation
paper.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled a shift from sentence-level to document-to-document (Doc2Doc) machine translation, promising improved global coherence. However, document-to-document generation in a single pass frequently suffers from structural misalignment, manifesting as sentence omissions or hallucinations that violate the core requirement of source-target correspondence. To address this, we introduce Sentence Translation Alignment Rate (STAR), an auxiliary metric that explicitly quantifies sentence-level structural fidelity. Building on this, we propose STAR-masked Preference Optimization (StarPO), a framework that ranks document-level hypotheses by structural quality and utilizes a dynamic alignment mask to focus optimization on misaligned segments. Experimental results across news and literary domains demonstrate that StarPO significantly enhances translation quality and structural integrity. Notably, StarPO allows compact models to surpass the performance of massive proprietary systems like GPT-4o while maintaining superior token efficiency.

analysis.problem_statement: Document-to-document machine translation using Large Language Models often suffers from structural misalignment, such as sentence omissions or hallucinations, which violates the required source-target correspondence.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Structural fidelity and alignment consistency in long-context generation.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical issue of structural drift in Doc2Doc translation by introducing a metric (STAR) and an optimization framework (StarPO) that explicitly enforce sentence-level alignment. By focusing optimization on misaligned segments, it enables compact open-source models to outperform massive proprietary systems like GPT-4o in both quality and structural integrity.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Translation quality and structural integrity (Sentence Translation Alignment Rate)
key_metrics.baseline: GPT-4o and other massive proprietary systems

technical_breakdown.method: Introduces STAR as an auxiliary metric to quantify structural fidelity and StarPO, a preference optimization framework that ranks hypotheses by structural quality.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Preference Optimization framework with a dynamic alignment mask component.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses a dynamic alignment mask to focus optimization specifically on misaligned segments during the training process.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not specified in summary

paper.title: Learning New Facts with QLoRA: An Acquisition-Retention Frontier
paper.summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning is often assumed to preserve pretrained capabilities because it updates only a small number of parameters. We show that this assumption depends strongly on adapter capacity. We study factual acquisition in a controlled OpenStreetMap-derived benchmark where Qwen3-4B must acquire anonymized geographic associations while retaining unrelated capabilities. Comparing full fine-tuning (FFT) with quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) at ranks 8, 16, 32, and 64, we find that rank induces a clear acquisition--retention frontier. Low-rank QLoRA preserves out-of-domain (OOD) performance but acquires fewer facts, whereas higher ranks improve same-fact paraphrase generalization at an increasing cost in performance on unrelated benchmarks. FFT behaves as a conservative baseline: it retains general capabilities well, but does not reach the highest factual-acquisition regime. Distributional, weight-space, and spectral diagnostics mirror this behavioral trade-off, with higher-rank QLoRA moving farther from the pretrained model. A separate math adaptation experiment shows a weaker frontier, suggesting that the effect is most pronounced when adaptation must install new factual associations rather than reinforce skills already supported by pretraining. Code and data are available at https://github.com/zhngstl/new_facts_forgetting.

analysis.problem_statement: The paper investigates the trade-off between acquiring new factual knowledge and retaining pre-existing capabilities in parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), specifically challenging the assumption that low-rank adapters inherently preserve pretrained knowledge.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Catastrophic forgetting and the capacity-accuracy trade-off in parameter-efficient fine-tuning for factual knowledge injection.
analysis.executive_summary: This work demonstrates that the common belief that QLoRA preserves pretrained capabilities is conditional on adapter rank, revealing a distinct acquisition-retention frontier. It provides empirical evidence that higher ranks are necessary for robust factual generalization but come at the cost of degrading unrelated out-of-domain performance, offering critical guidance for balancing knowledge injection with model stability.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Acquisition-Retention Frontier (trade-off between new fact acquisition and OOD retention)
key_metrics.metric_value: Qualitative frontier observed across ranks 8, 16, 32, and 64; no single scalar improvement value provided in summary
key_metrics.baseline: Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) and lower-rank QLoRA variants

technical_breakdown.method: Controlled benchmarking of Qwen3-4B using an OpenStreetMap-derived dataset to measure factual acquisition (anonymized geographic associations) against retention of unrelated capabilities, comparing FFT and QLoRA at varying ranks.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Qwen3-4B base model with QLoRA adapters (ranks 8, 16, 32, 64) and Full Fine-Tuning variants.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Use of distributional, weight-space, and spectral diagnostics to correlate behavioral trade-offs with model distance from the pretrained state; specific focus on same-fact paraphrase generalization.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not specified in summary; code available at https://github.com/zhngstl/new_facts_forgetting

paper.title: Unifying Detection and Adaptation in Task-Free Continual Learning
paper.summary: To mitigate catastrophic forgetting in downstream continual learning (CL) for large language models (LLMs), existing methods typically constrain parameter updates or introduce task-specific adaptation modules. However, these methods often rely on explicit task boundaries during training, limiting their applicability to realistic task-free scenarios. In this paper, we propose a \textbf{Fi}sher-guided \textbf{uni}fied (\textbf{FiUni}) framework for batch-level task detection and parameter-efficient continual adaptation. FiUni is motivated by a key observation about the Fisher information matrix (FIM) of pre-trained models: the orthogonality among the principal subspaces of its Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (K-FAC) approximation, estimated from a small number of downstream task samples, can reflect the similarity between different tasks. Based on this observation, FiUni constructs FIM-derived frozen subspaces to guide low-rank adaptation (LoRA), while matching the Fisher principal subspace of each incoming batch window with historical subspaces. This enables FiUni to adaptively determine whether to reuse existing knowledge, expand a related subspace, or create a new subspace, dynamically balancing knowledge sharing and task isolation. Experiments show that FiUni can effectively infer latent batch-level task affiliations and achieve competitive performance against advanced task-aware CL methods with fewer trainable parameters.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing continual learning methods for LLMs rely on explicit task boundaries, limiting their applicability to realistic task-free scenarios where task identities are unknown.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Catastrophic forgetting in task-free continual learning without explicit task boundaries.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical gap between theoretical continual learning methods that require known task boundaries and real-world applications where tasks are unlabeled. By leveraging Fisher information to detect task similarity at the batch level, it enables dynamic, parameter-efficient adaptation that balances knowledge sharing and isolation.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Competitive performance against advanced task-aware CL methods with fewer trainable parameters
key_metrics.baseline: Advanced task-aware continual learning methods

technical_breakdown.method: FiUni uses the orthogonality of principal subspaces from the Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (K-FAC) approximation of the Fisher Information Matrix to infer batch-level task affiliations and guide low-rank adaptation.
technical_breakdown.architecture: FiUni framework with FIM-derived frozen subspaces guiding LoRA, matching incoming batch windows with historical subspaces to decide between reusing, expanding, or creating new subspaces.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: K-FAC approximation of FIM, low-rank adaptation (LoRA), batch-level task detection via subspace orthogonality matching.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Parameter-efficient with fewer trainable parameters than baselines; computational cost dominated by FIM estimation from small sample sets.

paper.title: Research Design Tracking and Assessment for the Social Sciences
paper.summary: Reliable assessment of causal research designs in the social sciences is critical for evidence-based policy-making, yet has so far relied entirely on manual expert analysis. We introduce Automated Research Design Tracking and Assessment (ARDTrA), a task that involves detecting the research design used in a paper and assessing the quality of its application. We create an expert-annotated dataset of papers covering six families of counterfactual research designs and evaluate the task using a multi-turn RAG-based conversational pipeline. Across four retrieval strategies, four LLMs and six embedding models, we find that passage length is the main driver of performance, explaining 52-66% of the variance. A per-research-design analysis also shows that human and machine difficulty do not align: the designs that prove hardest for the system are not those on which expert annotators disagree most, pointing to two independent sources of task difficulty.
paper.comment: Paper accepted at EMNLP 2026 - Main Conference

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the lack of automated, reliable methods for detecting and assessing the quality of causal research designs in social science literature, which currently relies on manual expert analysis.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Automated domain-specific evaluation and structured information extraction from unstructured academic text.
analysis.executive_summary: This work introduces ARDTrA, a benchmark for automated assessment of causal research designs, highlighting that passage length is the primary driver of performance in RAG-based pipelines. It reveals a misalignment between human and machine difficulty, suggesting distinct sources of error in automated scientific assessment.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Variance explained by passage length in model performance
key_metrics.baseline: Multi-turn RAG-based conversational pipeline across four retrieval strategies, four LLMs, and six embedding models

technical_breakdown.method: Multi-turn RAG-based conversational pipeline for detecting research design and assessing application quality.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system with multiple retrieval strategies, LLM backends, and embedding models.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Expert-annotated dataset covering six families of counterfactual research designs; evaluation across four retrieval strategies, four LLMs, and six embedding models.

paper.title: Cascaded Batch Prompting
paper.summary: Although batch prompting makes large language model inference more efficient by processing multiple instances simultaneously, it suffers from unpredictable downstream task performance. We propose cascaded batch prompting, a two-stage approach designed to resolve the unpredictability of conventional batch prompting by disentangling complex reasoning from symbol grounding. Experiments on multiple-choice question answering and natural language inference demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms the standard single prompting baseline while achieving a speedup proportional to batch size, establishing a new state of the art on the Pareto frontier.

analysis.problem_statement: Conventional batch prompting for large language models suffers from unpredictable downstream task performance due to the entanglement of complex reasoning and symbol grounding within a single inference step.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Inference reliability and efficiency trade-off in batch processing
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the instability of batch prompting by introducing a two-stage method that separates reasoning from symbol grounding. It demonstrates that this approach maintains high accuracy while achieving linear speedups relative to batch size, effectively improving the Pareto frontier for LLM inference efficiency.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Performance on multiple-choice question answering and natural language inference with speedup proportional to batch size
key_metrics.baseline: Standard single prompting baseline

technical_breakdown.method: Cascaded batch prompting, a two-stage approach that disentangles complex reasoning from symbol grounding to resolve unpredictability.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Two-stage pipeline: Stage 1 handles complex reasoning, Stage 2 handles symbol grounding.

paper.title: MVC-Bench: Benchmarking Calibration of Medical Vision-Language Models
paper.summary: Reliable evaluation of vision-language models (VLMs) and medical vision-language models (Medical-VLMs) requires calibrated confidence, particularly under realistic clinical conditions. However, existing efforts mainly focused on improving accuracy, leaving calibration in the medical domain underexplored. To this end, we propose MVC-Bench, a calibration-centric benchmark for medical image classification with VLMs and Medical-VLMs. MVC-Bench assesses the calibration across three axes: (i) robustness to modality, backbone, and domain shift (ii) effectiveness of calibration strategies and prompt-tuning methods (iii) stability under prompt-template and random-seed variations. The benchmark covers eight different backbones, three medical modalities, including fundus imaging, histopathology, and chest X-ray under in-domain and domain shift settings. It compares post-hoc calibration, train-time calibration, and zero-shot inference methods, together with six prompt-tuning methods. Across more than 1638 controlled experiments, we report accuracy and Expected Calibration Error (ECE) as primary metrics, and further report results with complementary calibration measures, including Maximum Calibration Error (MCE) and Adaptive Calibration Error (ACE). We further investigate the underlying causes of miscalibration in VLMs and Medical-VLMs and propose a simple train-time calibration method, Multi-Class Margin (MCM) regularization, which achieves lowest ECE on 10 out of 12 settings in in-domain and remains competitive under domain shifts. Collectively, MVC-Bench provides a structured evaluation framework and actionable guidance for improving calibration in safety-critical medical workflows.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing evaluations of medical vision-language models (Medical-VLMs) prioritize accuracy while neglecting the critical need for calibrated confidence scores in safety-critical clinical settings.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Reliability and Trustworthiness (Calibration)
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the gap in evaluating the calibration of Medical-VLMs, which is essential for safe deployment in clinical workflows where model uncertainty must be accurately quantified. By introducing a comprehensive benchmark that tests robustness across modalities, backbones, and domain shifts, it provides a structured framework for assessing model reliability beyond mere accuracy.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Expected Calibration Error (ECE)
key_metrics.metric_value: Lowest ECE in 10 out of 12 in-domain settings
key_metrics.baseline: Post-hoc calibration, train-time calibration, and zero-shot inference methods
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: Not explicitly quantified in percentage, but reported as lowest ECE in 10/12 settings

technical_breakdown.method: The paper proposes MVC-Bench, a calibration-centric benchmark, and Multi-Class Margin (MCM) regularization, a train-time calibration method.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Evaluates eight different backbones across three medical modalities (fundus imaging, histopathology, chest X-ray) under in-domain and domain shift settings.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Compares post-hoc, train-time, and zero-shot calibration methods alongside six prompt-tuning techniques. MCM regularization is used to improve calibration during training.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Involves over 1638 controlled experiments, suggesting significant computational resources for benchmarking, but MCM is described as a 'simple' train-time method.

paper.title: ASIL: Replacing Screenshot-and-Click with Structured State and Semantic Actions
paper.summary: Powerful code agents can execute scripts, call tools, and manage files, yet many important applications remain accessible primarily through graphical user interfaces. We argue that screenshot-and-click is an inefficient interface for software-operating agents: screenshots are state-incomplete, and GUI actions are brittle, semantically weak, and poorly matched to long-horizon planning. We introduce ASIL (Agent-Software Interaction Layer), an agent-native interface that exposes software through structured JSON observations and code-executable semantic actions, realized through the deepest feasible access path for each application. We instantiate ASIL across 15 applications and a benchmark of 300 single-application and 80 multi-application tasks. ASIL reaches above 80 with closed models while executing fewer than five actions per task. Under a repaired runtime and a 50-step screenshot budget, the same tasks yield 6.6 and 26.6 strict success under screenshot-and-click control, rising to 15.0 and 53.3 on an easier OSWorld-comparable band. Against application-native interfaces on matched tasks, ASIL exceeds LibreOffice's UNO API by 28-38 strict points but only matches draw.io's MCP content contract. The structured modality also suits training: small-scale SFT raises Qwen3.5-2B from 58.0 to 72.1 and Qwen3.5-9B from 66.6 to 80.4, and resource-limited on-policy RL further raises them to 74.4 and 82.2.
paper.comment: Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026. 19 pages, 7 figures: 9-page main paper followed by limitations, ethics, acknowledgments, references, and appendices A-E. Project page: https://sharryxr.github.io/ASIL/

analysis.problem_statement: Current GUI agents rely on inefficient and brittle screenshot-and-click interfaces that provide incomplete state information and semantically weak actions, hindering long-horizon planning.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Inefficient and brittle interaction between AI agents and graphical user interfaces (GUIs) due to reliance on visual perception and low-level pixel-based actions.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper introduces ASIL, an agent-native interface that replaces visual screenshots with structured JSON observations and semantic, code-executable actions. By leveraging the deepest feasible access path for applications, it significantly improves task success rates and efficiency, reducing the number of actions required per task compared to traditional GUI automation.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Strict success rate on single-application and multi-application tasks
key_metrics.baseline: Screenshot-and-click control and application-native interfaces (e.g., LibreOffice UNO API)
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: 28-38 points higher than LibreOffice UNO API; significant increase over screenshot-and-click (e.g., 6.6 to >80)

technical_breakdown.architecture: Agent-Software Interaction Layer (ASIL) instantiated across 15 applications, supporting both single and multi-application tasks.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses structured JSON for state representation and semantic actions for execution; evaluated on a benchmark of 300 single-app and 80 multi-app tasks; includes SFT and on-policy RL for model training.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Executes fewer than five actions per task; training involves small-scale SFT and resource-limited on-policy RL on Qwen3.5 models.

paper.title: RubricRM: Generative Reward Modeling via Dynamic Rubrics for Image Generation and Editing
paper.summary: Reward models play an essential role in aligning visual generative models, yet most existing visual reward models use a single scalar score or rely on fixed criteria that cannot adapt to different instructions. This limits both interpretability and task sensitivity, especially for text-to-image generation and instruction-based image editing, where different inputs require different evaluation dimensions. We propose RubricRM, a pairwise generative reward modeling framework that first produces an input-specific rubric with evaluation dimensions, weights, and scoring criteria, and then applies the rubric to score candidate images. We train dedicated RubricRM models for text-to-image generation and image editing using a two-stage training pipeline: supervised fine-tuning teaches the model the rubric-based scoring paradigm, while GRPO further improves scoring through fine-grained dimension-level rewards. Experiments on multiple generation and editing benchmarks show that RubricRM outperforms existing specialized reward models and remains competitive with strong proprietary MLLM judges despite using smaller backbones. Our models, data, and code are available at https://github.com/zijiankan/RubricRM.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing visual reward models rely on static scalar scores or fixed criteria, limiting their interpretability and ability to adapt evaluation dimensions to diverse text-to-image and image editing instructions.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Lack of task-specific adaptability and interpretability in visual reward modeling for generative AI alignment.
analysis.executive_summary: RubricRM introduces a dynamic, input-specific rubric generation mechanism that allows reward models to tailor evaluation criteria to individual prompts, enhancing alignment precision for visual generation tasks. By combining supervised fine-tuning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) at the dimension level, it achieves performance competitive with large proprietary MLLMs while using smaller, more efficient backbones.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Outperformance of specialized reward models and competitiveness with proprietary MLLM judges
key_metrics.baseline: Existing specialized visual reward models and strong proprietary MLLM judges

technical_breakdown.method: A pairwise generative reward modeling framework that first generates an input-specific rubric (dimensions, weights, criteria) and then scores candidate images against this rubric.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Dedicated models for text-to-image and image editing, utilizing smaller backbones compared to proprietary MLLMs.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Two-stage training pipeline: 1) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) to learn the rubric-based scoring paradigm; 2) Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to refine scoring using fine-grained dimension-level rewards.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not explicitly stated, but implies standard LLM/MLLM training overhead with an additional generation step for rubrics and a policy optimization phase.

paper.title: From Atomic to Agentic: Towards Interpretable Evaluation of LLMs' Agentic Mathematical Capabilities
paper.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are evolving from performing end-to-end mathematical reasoning to integrating agentic intelligence. However, most existing math benchmarks evaluate only final answers. This outcome-oriented evaluation provides limited diagnostic value for identifying process-level failures or rigorous logic, failing to guide the transformation of LLMs into robust agents. To bridge this gap, we present a process-level benchmark designed to evaluate the inherent agentic mathematical reasoning abilities of LLMs. Our framework aligns problem-solving agentic behaviors with a structured taxonomy of reusable mathematical atomic capabilities. We design a comprehensive suite of planning, action, and feedback tasks across both textual and multimodal contexts, supported by an automated pipeline that synthesizes high-quality trajectories and produces fine-grained annotations via controlled LLM rewriting. Experiments reveal that models with similar end-to-end accuracy can exhibit markedly different agentic capability profiles. This demonstrates that process-level evaluation is crucial for interpreting the true potential of LLMs and guiding the development of next-generation mathematical agents.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing mathematical benchmarks for LLMs rely on outcome-oriented evaluation (final answers), which fails to provide diagnostic insight into process-level failures or the specific agentic capabilities required for robust mathematical reasoning.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Lack of process-level interpretability and diagnostic granularity in evaluating LLM agentic behaviors and mathematical reasoning trajectories.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical gap in evaluating LLMs as agents by moving beyond final-answer accuracy to assess intermediate reasoning steps. It introduces a process-level benchmark that maps agentic behaviors to a taxonomy of atomic mathematical capabilities, revealing that models with similar end-to-end performance can have vastly different underlying agentic profiles. This distinction is vital for guiding the development of next-generation mathematical agents that are not just accurate but also robust and interpretable.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Divergence in agentic capability profiles among models with similar end-to-end accuracy
key_metrics.metric_value: Not explicitly quantified in summary (qualitative finding of 'markedly different' profiles)
key_metrics.baseline: Standard end-to-end mathematical benchmarks (outcome-oriented)
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: N/A (Diagnostic benchmark, not a performance optimization paper)

technical_breakdown.method: The authors propose a process-level benchmark framework that aligns agentic problem-solving behaviors with a structured taxonomy of reusable mathematical atomic capabilities. They synthesize high-quality trajectories and generate fine-grained annotations using an automated pipeline based on controlled LLM rewriting.
technical_breakdown.architecture: A structured taxonomy of atomic mathematical capabilities integrated with a suite of planning, action, and feedback tasks. The system supports both textual and multimodal contexts and includes an automated data synthesis and annotation pipeline.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Utilizes controlled LLM rewriting to produce fine-grained annotations and synthesize trajectories. The benchmark suite is designed to evaluate specific agentic behaviors (planning, action, feedback) rather than just final outputs.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not specified in the provided metadata. The focus is on benchmark construction and evaluation methodology rather than model training complexity.

paper.title: RuleWeaver: Benchmarking Rule-Centered Scenario Reasoning for Large Language Models
paper.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to specialized domains, where effective use of domain expertise often requires reasoning over complex rules in concrete scenarios. However, existing benchmarks only partially evaluate this capability, as they either focus on output-level instruction constraints or overlook the distinct roles that rules play in scenario reasoning. To address these gaps, this paper introduces RuleWeaver, a benchmark construction framework for evaluating rule-centered scenario reasoning. RuleWeaver starts from corpus-derived IF-THEN Meta Rules, progressively augments them into complex rules, and composes these rules into rule-centered scenario QA instances. Beyond final-answer correctness, RuleWeaver further supports process-level evaluation through rubric-based answer quality, rule recall, and rule precision. Experiments on 11 representative LLMs show that current models still struggle with complex rule-centered scenario reasoning, with even the best-performing model achieving only around 50% of the maximum rubric score. We make our code and dataset available here: https://github.com/SharkSpicy-NLP/RuleWeaver.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing benchmarks fail to adequately evaluate Large Language Models' ability to reason over complex, multi-step domain-specific rules within concrete scenarios, often conflating rule adherence with general instruction following.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Lack of fine-grained, process-level evaluation metrics for rule-based logical reasoning and domain-specific compliance in LLMs.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the gap in evaluating LLMs' capacity for rule-centered scenario reasoning, a critical skill for specialized domain applications. By introducing a framework that decomposes reasoning into rule recall and precision, it provides a more rigorous assessment than simple output correctness. The findings reveal that even state-of-the-art models struggle with complex rule interactions, achieving only ~50% of maximum quality scores.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Rubric-based answer quality score (process-level evaluation)
key_metrics.baseline: 11 representative Large Language Models
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: N/A (Benchmark paper, not a model improvement paper)

technical_breakdown.method: A benchmark construction framework that derives IF-THEN Meta Rules from corpora, augments them into complex rules, and composes them into scenario-based QA instances.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Pipeline consisting of rule derivation, rule augmentation, and scenario composition modules, coupled with a multi-dimensional evaluation system (final answer, rule recall, rule precision, rubric quality).
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses corpus-derived IF-THEN Meta Rules as the atomic unit; applies progressive augmentation to increase rule complexity; evaluates via rubric-based scoring rather than just exact match.
