analysis.bottleneck_addressed: High latency and computational cost of traditional OCR-based ingestion and retrieval for visual documents, which hinders real-time updates in dynamic enterprise environments.
analysis.executive_summary: PULSAR addresses the critical gap in enterprise RAG for visual documents by replacing costly OCR pipelines with a vision-first, late-interaction retrieval system. It significantly reduces latency and ingestion costs while maintaining high retrieval accuracy, enabling real-time access to frequently updated financial and diligence materials.

technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses ColPali-style backbone, MaxSim rescoring, and pooled representations to reduce vector search dimensions. Deployed at Mubadala Investment Company.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Reduces computational load by 15.1x in latency and 20x in ingestion cost per page compared to OCR+verbalization. Sustains 88x higher QPS under concurrent load.

paper.title: DARTS: Decoder-Aware Representation Tuning via Surgery for Model Merging
paper.summary: Model merging combines multiple task-specific fine-tuned LLMs into a single multi-task model without additional training. However, merged models are known to suffer from representation bias: systematic drift between the merged model's hidden states and those of each individual source model. Prior work (Yang et al., 2024a) study and mitigate this bias for encoder-based vision models using a lightweight correction module trained with L1 loss. However, such bias is not studied for decoder models due to their autoregressive nature. We analyze the problem of representation bias in decoder models, and show two challenges absent in encoders: (1) the causal attention mask causes bias to accumulate across token positions, requiring position-dependent correction; and (2) not all token positions are equally important, i.e., high-entropy (decision-critical) positions matter far more than low-entropy ones. To address these challenges, we propose Decoder-Aware Representation Tuning via Surgery (DARTS). DARTS employs a novel entropy-weighted L1 loss to upweight correction at high-entropy positions where errors most affect generation quality, and a per-position additive bias that captures position-dependent error without overparameterization. We perform extensive evaluation on three domains: code generation (HumanEval), mathematical reasoning (GSM8K), and instruction following (AlpacaEval) on Llama-2-7B models, and show DARTS achieves significant improvement over the standard surgery approach while adding negligible parameters ($0.1\%$ of total parameters).

analysis.problem_statement: Merged decoder-based LLMs suffer from representation bias where hidden states drift from source models, causing performance degradation that is exacerbated by causal attention accumulation and varying token importance.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Model merging efficiency and multi-task capability without additional training
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical limitation of model merging in autoregressive LLMs, where standard correction methods fail due to the causal nature of attention. By introducing position-aware and entropy-weighted corrections, it enables more effective combination of specialized models, reducing the need for expensive retraining while maintaining high performance across diverse tasks.

key_metrics.metric_value: Negligible parameter overhead (0.1% of total parameters)
key_metrics.baseline: Standard surgery approach (Yang et al., 2024a)

technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Entropy-weighted L1 loss function; per-position additive bias vector; evaluated on Llama-2-7B across HumanEval, GSM8K, and AlpacaEval.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Negligible computational overhead, adding only 0.1% of total model parameters.

paper.title: Acquire, Repair, Preserve: A Diagnosis-Guided Post-Training Recipe for Small-Model Dialogue Game Agents
paper.summary: Interactive dialogue games test a capability that static benchmarks largely leave implicit: a model must carry state across turns, interpret feedback, and choose valid actions under changing constraints. We study this setting in the LM Playschool Challenge with a 2B open-weight model, and find that many failures are not only broad knowledge failures but also local decision failures: repeated guesses, malformed actions, and violations of feedback that the model has just seen. These diagnostics motivate a training recipe organized around three steps: acquire broad game participation through supervised fine-tuning, repair mechanically verifiable failures within one targeted dialogue-game family using turn-local preference pairs, and preserve general capabilities beyond these dialogue games. In the official final evaluation, our submission improves public clemscore from 10.67 to 38.92 and closed in-domain score from 13.41 to 41.17, while approximately preserving aggregate static performance (44.14 vs. 44.24 for the baseline). Out-of-domain clemscore remains low at 7.88, with the largest gains concentrated in unseen variants of the targeted family. Our results suggest that broad SFT brings most of the model's capability improvement; turn-local supervision can be effective when failure detection is precise, with observed transfer concentrated primarily within-family.

analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Local decision failures and state management in small models during multi-turn interactive tasks, specifically addressing issues like repeated guesses and malformed actions that static benchmarks fail to capture.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper demonstrates that a diagnosis-guided post-training recipe (SFT, targeted preference optimization, and preservation) can significantly enhance the interactive game-playing capabilities of small models. It highlights that while broad supervised fine-tuning provides the majority of capability gains, turn-local preference pairs are effective for repairing specific, mechanically verifiable failures within a targeted domain.

paper.title: LongPIBench: A Long-Context Benchmark for Prompt Injection
paper.summary: Prompt injection attacks pose a serious security risk to large language models in real-world applications. However, existing prompt injection benchmarks primarily focus on short-context inputs, leaving the attacks and defenses in long-context settings largely unexplored. This gap leads to a substantial overestimation of the effectiveness of current defenses. In this paper, we bridge the gap by introducing LongPIBench, a long-context benchmark for prompt injection covering 4 realistic application scenarios: paper peer review, resume screening, code review, and email summary. For each scenario, we construct a synthetic dataset and a real-world dataset, with context lengths ranging from thousands to tens of thousands of tokens. The evaluation results on LongPIBench reveal significant vulnerabilities of prompt injection defenses under long-context settings: even simple heuristic prompt injection attacks achieve high success rates and frequently bypass state-of-the-art defenses. We hope LongPIBench can serve as a practical benchmark for systematically evaluating prompt injection defenses in realistic long-context scenarios.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses a critical blind spot in LLM security by demonstrating that defenses effective in short-context scenarios often fail when context lengths extend to tens of thousands of tokens. By introducing LongPIBench, it provides a realistic evaluation framework for common enterprise tasks like code review and email summarization, revealing that simple heuristic attacks can still bypass state-of-the-art defenses in long-document scenarios.

paper.title: CamoDocs: A Poisoning Attack Against Retrieval-Augmented Language Models Using Camouflaged Documents
paper.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) augments LLMs with external documents, but public or user-editable sources expose RAG systems to data poisoning: attackers can inject malicious documents to steer outputs toward targeted answers. Existing poisoning attacks often rely on query inclusion, inserting the target query into poisoned documents to improve retrieval; however, this creates lexical and embedding-space artifacts that make them easy to filter. We propose CamoDocs, a poisoning attack that avoids direct query inclusion by camouflaging adversarial documents among benign content. CamoDocs chunks synthesized benign and adversarial drafts, replaces selected tokens in benign chunks with dispersion tokens that spread poisoned-document embeddings, and applies coherence filtering to limit readability degradation. Across seven RAG defenses, three open-weight LLMs, and three benchmarks, CamoDocs achieves strong average ASR while avoiding query-overlap artifacts exploited by simple query detection. It also remains effective against proprietary models, achieving average ASRs of 61.80% on GPT-5.4-mini and 55.09% on Claude-Haiku-4.5. Finally, we show that erasure-heavy clustering defenses such as TrustRAG can reduce ASR, but only with substantial utility drops on retrieval-dependent benchmarks such as NeoQA. Code is available at https://github.com/jaewonalive/CamoDocs.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing data poisoning attacks against Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are easily detectable and filterable because they rely on direct query inclusion, creating lexical and embedding-space artifacts.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Security vulnerability in RAG systems due to the detectability of adversarial documents in public or user-editable knowledge bases.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper introduces CamoDocs, a stealthy poisoning attack that evades standard query-overlap detection by camouflaging malicious content within benign documents using dispersion tokens. It demonstrates significant attack success rates against both open-weight and proprietary LLMs, highlighting a critical gap in current RAG defense mechanisms that rely on simple lexical filtering.

key_metrics.baseline: Standard RAG defenses and simple query detection filters

technical_breakdown.architecture: A pre-processing pipeline for document poisoning that integrates coherence filtering to maintain readability while embedding adversarial signals.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses dispersion tokens to manipulate embedding space, applies coherence filtering to limit readability degradation, and avoids lexical overlap with target queries.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not specified in the abstract; involves document synthesis, token replacement, and filtering steps prior to ingestion into the RAG system.

paper.title: GRACE:Gradient-guided Coreset Selection for LLM Unlearning
paper.summary: Machine Unlearning methods for Large Language Models typically assume pre-specified forget and retain sets. In realistic settings, however, requests may provide only a few examples of undesired behavior, requiring forget and retain sets to be inferred from heterogeneous corpora. We study this data-selection problem and propose GRACE , a gradient-guided coreset selection method that constructs both forget and retain sets for LLM unlearning. GRACE first computes a forget direction from seed examples that elicit the undesired behavior, then selects a compact forget coreset whose gradients approximate this direction using non-negative orthogonal matching pursuit. To preserve model utility, it selects retain examples after projecting out the forget direction and applying clustered orthogonal matching pursuit in the remaining gradient space. Across two target domains, two model families, and four unlearning algorithms, GRACE improves model utility while maintaining comparable forget quality, with particularly consistent gains over prior gradient-based selection methods.
paper.comment: 20 pages, 16 tables, 5 figures, accepted to EMNLP Findings

analysis.problem_statement: How to automatically infer optimal forget and retain data coresets from heterogeneous corpora when only a few seed examples of undesired behavior are provided, rather than relying on pre-specified datasets.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Data curation and selection for machine unlearning, specifically the lack of scalable methods to derive representative training subsets from large, unstructured corpora without manual annotation.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses a critical gap in LLM unlearning by automating the selection of data subsets, which is currently a manual and error-prone process. By using gradient-guided coreset selection, it enables more practical and scalable unlearning workflows where specific 'forget' and 'retain' sets are not explicitly defined, thereby improving model utility while maintaining effective unlearning.

key_metrics.baseline: Prior gradient-based selection methods

technical_breakdown.method: GRACE computes a forget direction from seed examples and uses non-negative orthogonal matching pursuit to select a compact forget coreset that approximates this direction. paper.title: Stay Within Your Bounds: Distance-Guided Decoding for Guaranteed Context-Free Grammar Compliance
paper.summary: Grammar-constrained decoding helps large language models produce syntactically valid structured outputs, such as code, JSON, and SQL. For context-free grammars, many practical decoders enforce local prefix feasibility: each token must keep the current prefix extendable to some valid completion. Yet, under tokenizer-grammar mismatch and finite token budgets, feasible prefixes may still fail to reach acceptance. We propose a lookahead-guided decoding framework for context-free grammars based on pushdown automata. Offline, we compute bounded pushdown summaries with reachability labels and upper-bound distances to acceptance. Online, these estimates guide horizon-aware pruning and beam search. The resulting decoder is syntactically sound: every output is accepted by the target grammar. Experiments on JSON, SQL, and Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) show both consistent syntactic validity and improved completion quality over existing baselines.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing grammar-constrained decoders for context-free grammars often fail to produce valid completions within finite token budgets due to tokenizer-grammar mismatches, despite maintaining local prefix feasibility.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Reliability and syntactic validity of structured output generation in Large Language Models.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical failure mode where LLMs generate syntactically invalid structured data (JSON, SQL, LTL) due to the gap between tokenization and grammar rules. By introducing a lookahead-guided decoding framework that guarantees acceptance, it ensures that every generated output is syntactically sound, which is essential for reliable integration of LLMs into downstream applications requiring strict format compliance.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Consistent syntactic validity and improved completion quality
key_metrics.baseline: Existing grammar-constrained decoding baselines

technical_breakdown.method: A lookahead-guided decoding framework that uses offline-computed bounded pushdown summaries to guide online horizon-aware pruning and beam search.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Pushdown automata-based decoder with offline summary computation and online guided search.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Computes reachability labels and upper-bound distances to acceptance offline; uses these estimates for horizon-aware pruning and beam search online to ensure every output is accepted by the target grammar.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Involves offline computation of bounded pushdown summaries and online beam search with pruning; specific computational complexity metrics are not provided in the abstract.

paper.title: Twin Worlds: Equivariance-Based Abstention for Evidence-Grounded Reasoning
paper.summary: Knowledge-intensive reasoning requires Large Language Models (LLMs) to ground answers in provided evidence. When evidence is insufficient, it is desirable that models abstain rather than confidently generating unsupported answers. Existing abstention methods rely on uncertainty estimation or evidence sufficiency checks, but neither tests whether the reasoning process for generation, driven by the interaction of provided evidence and the model's internal memory parameters, is actually grounded in the evidence. A key contributing factor is that entity mentions in context activate memorised associations, causing models to generate plausible responses ungrounded in evidence. We propose Twin Worlds (TW), a framework for improving reliability in knowledge-intensive reasoning through equivariance-based abstention: unlike invariance, which requires outputs to remain unchanged, equivariance requires outputs to transform correspondingly under entity substitutions. A model grounded in the evidence should produce answers that shift consistently when entities are substituted while their relations are preserved. TW constructs multiple worlds via typed substitutions of the original input that preserve relational structure while reducing parametric priors, and uses equivariance violations as an abstention signal. Across four benchmarks and three model backbones, TW identifies when answers are not reliably grounded in the provided evidence and outperforms uncertainty- and sufficiency-based baselines.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing abstention methods for LLMs fail to verify if reasoning is grounded in provided evidence because entity mentions activate internal parametric memories, leading to confident but ungrounded generations when evidence is insufficient.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Hallucination and lack of evidence grounding in knowledge-intensive reasoning tasks.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical reliability gap where LLMs confidently generate answers based on internal memory rather than provided context. By introducing an equivariance-based abstention mechanism, it provides a robust method to detect when a model's reasoning is not actually grounded in the evidence, thereby improving the trustworthiness of AI systems in high-stakes knowledge-intensive applications.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Outperformance in identifying ungrounded answers compared to uncertainty- and sufficiency-based baselines.
key_metrics.baseline: Uncertainty estimation and evidence sufficiency checks

technical_breakdown.method: The framework constructs multiple 'twin worlds' via typed substitutions of entities in the input while preserving relational structure. It then checks for equivariance: if the model is grounded in evidence, its outputs should transform consistently under these substitutions. Violations of this equivariance property serve as the abstention signal.
technical_breakdown.architecture: A wrapper framework around existing LLM backbones that generates substituted input variants and compares output consistency.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses typed entity substitutions to reduce parametric priors while maintaining relational integrity; calculates equivariance violations as a metric for grounding.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Requires multiple forward passes per query (one for the original and one for each substituted 'twin world'), increasing inference latency but not requiring model retraining.

paper.title: GOD: Govern, Observe, and Direct - A Real-Time Control Room for Agent Societies
paper.summary: Generative-agent systems are easier to start than to inspect. A run can contain many agents, locations, messages, commands, and model calls, yet the operator often gets either a finished replay or raw logs. That makes it hard to ask why an agent moved, test a small intervention, or package a run for another researcher. GOD is a local-first control room for agent societies. From the same browser workflow, an operator can issue targeted questions or interventions and inspect the resulting replay state. The system combines a setup wizard, Agent Studio, Map Studio, a spatial replay interface, Ask and Intervene commands, and portable experiment, map, and agent packs. Its technical contribution is the command and artifact loop: live controls and replay evidence share the same operator command model, while package contracts separate scenario, map, and profile data from local runtime state. The public release includes hosted Smallville-style and PKU replays, the open-source repository, and downloadable packs. We evaluate this path on 15 completed run slots. Across the 14 intervention runs, 78 of 84 target-agent checks recorded the commanded destination, and 169 of 182 state answers matched a saved location or action string.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical gap in debugging and steering complex agent societies by providing a local-first control room that unifies live intervention with replay analysis. It is significant for the current AI landscape as it shifts agent development from a black-box execution model to a transparent, interactive engineering workflow, facilitating reproducibility and targeted debugging.

paper.title: SKILL.state: Scalable Long-Horizon Agent Skills
paper.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly act as autonomous agents executing complex, long-running procedural skills. Existing agent runtimes maintain execution by continually appending observations, actions, and intermediate reasoning traces to an ever-growing conversation history, causing latency degradation and context-poisoning failures over long horizons. We present SKILL.state, a runtime architecture that replaces append-only conversational history with an explicit, mutable execution state. At each execution step, the model receives only the immutable skill specification, the current structured execution state, and the latest observation. Intermediate reasoning is discarded immediately after producing a validated state update, preventing prompt growth with execution history. Across diverse datasets, models, and execution environments, SKILL. state improves task accuracy while substantially reducing cumulative token consumption. Our results demonstrate that explicit execution state is an effective and architecture-agnostic abstraction for scalable long-horizon agent skills.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing LLM agent runtimes suffer from latency degradation and context-poisoning failures due to the unbounded growth of append-only conversational histories during long-horizon tasks.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Context window limitations and cumulative token latency in long-horizon autonomous agents.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the scalability bottleneck of LLM agents by replacing unbounded conversation logs with a compact, mutable execution state. This architecture prevents prompt growth and context poisoning, enabling more reliable and cost-effective execution of complex, long-running procedural skills.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Task accuracy and cumulative token consumption
key_metrics.baseline: Append-only conversational history runtimes

technical_breakdown.method: The model receives only the immutable skill specification, current structured execution state, and latest observation at each step, discarding intermediate reasoning after state validation.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Runtime architecture utilizing explicit, mutable execution state instead of append-only history.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: State updates are validated before intermediate reasoning traces are discarded to prevent prompt growth.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Reduces cumulative token consumption and latency by limiting context size to current state and latest observation.

paper.title: CHISEL-ing Back Source Code with AI-enabled Iterative Recovery
paper.summary: Decompilation aims to recover high-level, compilable, and semantically equivalent code from binaries. Traditional decompilers produce pseudo-C that is difficult to read and does not compile, while the recent LLM-assisted approaches generate readable, but semantically incorrect code. LLM-aided iterative recovery is an emerging branch of research, but prior works rely on supplied test suites for semantic recovery. In this work, we present CHISEL, a test suite-free framework to iteratively recover source code from Ghidra-derived pseudo-C. CHISEL uses simple yet effective feedback from a compiler (static analysis) and a coverage-guided fuzzer (differential analysis), augmented by rich observables for grounded divergence detection and feedback, cross-iteration divergence memory, and best candidate retention. We systematically evaluate CHISEL for compilation and semantic recovery, feedback oracle soundness, and iteration overhead on 120 ExeBench functions compiled for the x86-64 architecture, across four optimizations (O0-O3), in both stripped and unstripped variants, using the open-weight Gemma4:31b LLM. CHISEL, with all recommended features, achieves an average of 96.1% re-compilability and 79.8% re-executability rates at an average of 2.1 iterations. Significantly, CHISEL recovers 26% of first-generation execution errors. At the same time, CHISEL feedback oracle falsely accepts only 9.4% candidates. Lastly, CHISEL performs significantly better than two recent prior work on LLM-assisted decompilation.

paper.title: Learning-Augmented Heuristics: Simple, yet Smart, Robust and Interpretable Cache Eviction
paper.summary: Caching is widely used across the system stack to improve performance and efficiency, with eviction algorithms at its core. Existing cache eviction policies fall into two broad categories: static heuristics (e.g., 2Q, S3-FIFO) and smart algorithms (e.g., ARC, LRB). Smart caches can adapt to workloads and have the potential to achieve higher efficiency and robustness than static heuristics. However, we find that existing smart caches suffer from objective mismatches and instability. We introduce Learning-Augmented Heuristics (LAH), a framework that learns the cache-level parameters of static heuristics. By decoupling the data and control planes, LAH supports simple, high-speed data reads and writes on the data plane, while performing occasional asynchronous learning on the control plane using cache-level features. We demonstrate the effectiveness of LAH through S4-FIFO, a Smart S3-FIFO cache eviction algorithm. We pre-train a single model on 4,140 production traces and embed it in S4-FIFO to learn optimal cache parameters. On 1,035 evaluation traces, S4-FIFO improves the mean efficiency by 26% compared to S3-FIFO and by 8% compared to 3L-Cache, the best state-of-the-art algorithm. S4-FIFO is also robust---increasing miss ratio over FIFO by 0.8% on the worst trace, whereas 3L-Cache increases FIFO's miss ratio by 8.8%. Finally, S4-FIFO's decisions are also interpretable: a language model can provide a rationale for why a particular configuration was chosen.

analysis.problem_statement: Existing smart cache eviction algorithms suffer from objective mismatches and instability, while static heuristics lack the adaptability to optimize performance across diverse workloads.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: System-level I/O efficiency and memory hierarchy optimization, specifically addressing the trade-off between the simplicity of static heuristics and the complexity/instability of adaptive smart caches.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper introduces Learning-Augmented Heuristics (LAH), a framework that decouples data and control planes to allow simple, fast cache operations while asynchronously learning optimal parameters. By applying this to S3-FIFO to create S4-FIFO, the system achieves superior efficiency and robustness compared to state-of-the-art algorithms like 3L-Cache. The approach is significant for high-performance computing and cloud infrastructure, as it provides an interpretable and robust method for optimizing memory usage without the overhead of complex adaptive algorithms.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Mean efficiency improvement in cache eviction
key_metrics.baseline: S3-FIFO and 3L-Cache (state-of-the-art)

technical_breakdown.method: The LAH framework learns cache-level parameters of static heuristics by decoupling the data plane (simple reads/writes) from the control plane (asynchronous learning using cache-level features).
technical_breakdown.architecture: A dual-plane architecture where the data plane handles high-speed operations with static logic, and the control plane runs a pre-trained model to adjust heuristic parameters asynchronously.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: S4-FIFO is implemented by embedding a single model pre-trained on 4,140 production traces into the S3-FIFO algorithm to learn optimal cache parameters. The system is evaluated on 1,035 traces.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Low data-plane complexity due to static heuristic execution; control-plane complexity is managed via asynchronous updates, allowing for high-speed I/O without blocking on learning computations.
